t: Bun.Image should support TIFF decoding on Linux
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
Bun.Image can identify TIFF input, but decoding TIFF is unsupported on Linux and returns ERR_IMAGE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED. The same API relies on native platform image backends on macOS and Windows, so behavior differs by deployment platform.
This prevents Linux server and Lambda applications that accept TIFF uploads from fully replacing Sharp. In my project, TIFF decoding is the only reason a Sharp/libvips fallback remains after migrating the rest of the image pipeline to Bun.Image.
The limitation is documented in Bun's platform backend table, but TIFF is already represented as an image format and detected by the runtime. A Linux decoder would make the API portable for this input format.
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
Add decode-only TIFF support to Bun.Image on Linux.
A portable TIFF decoder could feed Bun's existing decoded-pixel pipeline when no native Linux backend is available. Supporting the first image/page and normalizing it to Bun's existing RGBA8 representation would cover the common server-side ingestion case; TIFF encoding is not needed for this request.
Ideally this would work on the Linux targets commonly used for Bun deployments and Lambdas, including x64/arm64 and glibc/musl, while enforcing maxPixels before allocating the decoded output.
What alternatives have you considered?

Keep Sharp/libvips solely as a TIFF-to-PNG fallback. This works, but retains a large native dependency and its Lambda packaging/build complexity for one input format.
Reject TIFF uploads on Linux. This would regress an existing supported upload path.
Convert TIFF files in a separate service or external binary. This adds operational complexity and another runtime boundary for a conversion that otherwise belongs in the image pipeline.

t: Subprocess.kill(signalName) uses Linux signal numbers on macOS — "SIGUSR1" delivers SIGBUS (child "panics"), signalCode reporting also wrong
b:
ROOT CAUSE CORRECTION (deep-dived on main @ 892b1dab — the original analysis below is preserved but its mechanism was wrong):
The panic is not about signal delivery during streaming at all. It is:
Bun.Subprocess.kill(signalName) maps signal names with the LINUX signal-number table on macOS
src/bun_core/Global.rs — the canonical for_each_signal! X-macro that generates SignalCode — hardcodes Linux numbers unconditionally:
SIGBUS = 7, SIGFPE = 8, SIGKILL = 9, SIGUSR1 = 10, SIGSEGV = 11, SIGUSR2 = 12, ...
SIGCHLD = 17, SIGCONT = 18, SIGSTOP = 19, SIGTSTP = 20, ... SIGIO = 29, SIGPWR = 30, SIGSYS = 31
On Darwin (<sys/signal.h>): SIGUSR1=30, SIGUSR2=31, SIGBUS=10, SIGSYS=12, SIGURG=16, SIGSTOP=17, SIGTSTP=18, SIGCONT=19, SIGCHLD=20, SIGIO=23, SIGINFO=29, SIGEMT=7 — everything outside 1–6, 8, 9, 11, 13–15, 21–22, 24–28 diverges.
subprocess.kill("SIGUSR1") → FromJsEnum for bun_sys::SignalCode (src/jsc/lib.rs) → signal_code::from_name → 10 → kill(child, 10) = SIGBUS on macOS. Bun's crash reporter in the child catches the externally-sent SIGBUS with si_addr = 0 and prints panic: Bus error at address 0x0 — which is exactly the "panic" in my original report. The child's JS SIGUSR1 handler "never ran" because SIGUSR1 was never sent. The streaming response was a red herring (it merely made the child a Bun process someone wanted to signal gracefully).
Discriminating evidence (macOS 15.7.7 arm64, reproduces on 1.3.14 stable AND 1.4.0 canary 2892b1da)
A bash child that traps everything, signalled each way:
Subprocess.kill("SIGUSR1")     → child saw: GOT-BUS     ← Linux 10 = macOS SIGBUS
Subprocess.kill("SIGUSR2")     → child saw: GOT-SYS     ← Linux 12 = macOS SIGSYS
Subprocess.kill(30)            → child saw: GOT-USR1    ← numeric passes through correctly
Subprocess.kill("SIGTERM")     → child saw: GOT-TERM    ← 15 on both platforms, works
process.kill(pid, "SIGUSR1")   → child saw: GOT-USR1    ← process.kill maps correctly (separate path)
node:child_process .kill("SIGUSR1") → GOT-USR1          ← node-compat maps correctly (separate path)

And shell kill -USR1 <bun pid> is handled perfectly fine by process.on("SIGUSR1") even mid-stream — confirming signal delivery was never the bug.
Reverse direction is broken by the same table
A child killed by a real SIGUSR1 (/bin/kill -30) is reported as:
proc.signalCode === "SIGPWR"   // Linux name for 30; should be "SIGUSR1"
Worse cases in the same table

subprocess.kill("SIGCHLD") sends 17 = macOS SIGSTOP → silently stops the child

`http.Server` cannot adopt external sockets via `emit('connection')`
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
In latest bun canary there is massively improved support for new tls.TLSSocket which works great - thanks. This has almost unblocked our ability to run a node application on Bun, but there's one blocker remaining.
Node's http.Server has an internal connectionListener that attaches an
HTTPParser to every socket passed through the connection event. This
allows user code to feed arbitrary Duplex streams (e.g. a TLS-terminated
socket from a proxy) into http.createServer() by calling
server.emit('connection', socket).
Bun's http.Server does not have a JS-side connection listener. HTTP
parsing is done natively by uWS, and uWS only parses sockets that the
server itself accepted via listen(). Calling emit('connection', socket)
registers no parser on the socket — request events never fire.
Here is a reproduction:
bun-repro-emit-connection.js
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
Bun's http.Server (in _http_server.ts) registers no JS-side listener
for the connection event. Connections are instead delivered via the
native onServerConnection callback — uWS calls this directly when a
TCP connection arrives on the listening socket. The internal HTTP parser
and response pipeline are wired to the native uWS handle, not to an
abstract Duplex interface.
In Node, _http_server.js does:
this.on('connection', connectionListener);
Where connectionListener attaches an HTTPParser to the socket,
wires socket.on('data', …) → parser, and emits request when a
complete HTTP message is parsed. Any Duplex passed through the
connection event gets parsed.
What alternatives have you considered?
A workaround is to listen the http.Server on an ephemeral loopback port and pipe the decrypted stream through a net.connect() bridge — an extra TCP connection per tunnel.

t: process.binding("http_parser").methods contains "M - SEARCH" instead of "M-SEARCH"
b:
What version of Bun is running?
Verified on 1.3.14, and the root cause is still present on main.
What steps can reproduce the bug?
const { methods, allMethods } = process.binding("http_parser");
console.log(methods.includes("M-SEARCH"));   // false
console.log(methods.includes("M - SEARCH")); // true  ← note the spaces
What is the expected behavior?
process.binding("http_parser").methods (and allMethods) should contain the HTTP method token "M-SEARCH", matching:

the public require("node:http").METHODS, which is correct ("M-SEARCH"),
Node's process.binding("http_parser").methods,
the IANA/SSDP method token M-SEARCH (UPnP discovery).

What do you see instead?
The list contains the malformed "M - SEARCH" (spaces around the hyphen) instead of "M-SEARCH". Every other method matches Node.
Root cause
src/jsc/bindings/node/http/llhttp/llhttp.h (lines 356 and 409) has:
XX(24, MSEARCH, M - SEARCH)      \
Upstream llhttp (this file is vendored llhttp v9.3.0) defines it as XX(24, M_SEARCH, M-SEARCH). The extra spaces — most likely introduced by a clang-format pass treating - as a binary operator in the vendored macro table — get stringized by the C preprocessor into "M - SEARCH", which then flows into llhttp_method_name(24) and out through the process.binding("http_parser") compat layer.
M-SEARCH is the only hyphenated method in the table, so it's the only entry affected.
Suggested fix

In llhttp.h, restore M - SEARCH → M-SEARCH on both lines (and, since this is vendored, consider excluding src/jsc/bindings/node/http/llhttp/ from clang-format so it can't recur).
packages/bun-types/overrides.d.ts (lines 266 and 303) currently mirrors the typo in the methods/allMethods literal types — those "M - SEARCH" literals should be corrected to "M-SEARCH" in the same change so the types match the fixed runtime.

Bun's own HTTP server method handling (src/http_types/Method.rs) already uses the correct "M-SEARCH", so this is limited to the process.binding("http_parser") / node:http compat surface — but it's still a wrong method token there.

Bun.listen: NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 disables the default requestCert enforcement (same gap as #33754, missed by #33755's tests)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1+5b98630ac (repo checked out at feee846, current main as of this report)
What platform is your computer?
Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64
What steps can reproduce the bug?
This is the native Bun.listen()/Bun.connect() version of the node:tls bug in #35092, and it's related to #33754 (Bun.listen() does not enforce rejectUnauthorized, fixed by #33755), but it's a different, still-open gap in the same area.
Bun.listen({ tls: { requestCert: true } }) with rejectUnauthorized left unset is supposed to default to true, same as requestCert's documented behavior everywhere else in Bun. The default is computed in src/runtime/socket/SSLConfig.rs:
result.reject_unauthorized = generated
    .reject_unauthorized
    .unwrap_or_else(|| vm.get_tls_reject_unauthorized())
    as i32;
vm.get_tls_reject_unauthorized() reads NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED. This function builds the SSL config for both Bun.listen (server) and Bun.connect (client) - it has no is_server parameter, so it can't tell which role it's defaulting for. resolve_reject_unauthorized() (added by #33755, same file) then uses that value directly for the server's enforcement decision:
Some(cfg) => (!is_server || cfg.request_cert != 0) && cfg.reject_unauthorized != 0,
So a server with requestCert: true and no explicit rejectUnauthorized enforces correctly only as long as nothing in the process has set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 - a very common one-liner for working around a self-signed cert on some unrelated outbound request.

t: Bun.build: external ["node:zlib"] not honored when minify is enabled — polyfill bundled instead
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (0d9b296) — macOS arm64
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.x arm64
What steps can reproduce the bug?
entry.ts:
export async function go(data: Uint8Array): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  const { deflateSync } = await import("node:zlib");
  return new Uint8Array(deflateSync(data));
}
build.ts:
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ["entry.ts"],
  outdir: "out",
  format: "esm",
  target: "browser",
  minify: true,
  external: ["node:zlib"],
});
What is the expected behavior?
The await import("node:zlib") stays a runtime import in the output — which is exactly what happens when minify is omitted: grep -c "node:zlib" out/entry.js reports 1, and no zlib implementation is bundled.
What do you see instead?
With minify: true, the external import is replaced by Bun's bundled node:zlib browser polyfill: output grows from ~1 KB to ~260 KB (minified), and node:zlib no longer appears in the output at all. The externalization is silently dropped.
Granular isolation:

minify: { whitespace: true } → polyfill bundled, external broken
minify: { identifiers: true } → external honored
minify: { syntax: true } → external honored
external: ["node:zlib", "zlib"] and wildcard variants → still broken under minify

So the whitespace minifier specifically causes the external node: builtin to be replaced by the polyfill.
Additional information
Real-world impact: migrating a production esbuild build (--minify --external:node:zlib, 12 entry points) to Bun.build. The polyfill adds ~290–350 KB per affected bundle and changes a deliberate dual-environment fallback (CompressionStream in browsers, node:zlib elsewhere) — blocking the migration until externalization survives minification.

t: [Bug] Bun Windows - Stale process.env values from transpilation cache
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1+5b98630ac
What platform is your computer?
Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19044.0 x64
What steps can reproduce the bug?

Create a single file index.ts:

console.log("HOST:", process.env.DATABASE_HOST);

Create .env:

DATABASE_HOST="value-A"

Run it (establishes transpilation cache):

$ bun index.ts
HOST: value-A


Change .env without modifying any .ts file:

DATABASE_HOST="value-B"

Run again:

$ bun index.ts
HOST: value-A

The output is still value-A even though .env says value-B.


Even deleting .env entirely and running again still prints value-A, proving the value comes from a cached transpilation, not from the filesystem.


The only fix: modify any byte of index.ts (add a comment, then remove it), which forces re-transpilation and picks up the new .env value.


What is the expected behavior?
Each bun index.ts invocation starts a fresh process, reads .env from disk, and all process.env.* accesses happen at runtime. Changing .env should take effect on the next run.
What do you see instead?
process.env.* values are permanently baked into a transpilation cache keyed by source file content hash. Changing .env does not invalidate the cache. The application silently uses stale values with no warning or error.
Evidence table:

.env value

No
value-A (stale from cache)

Additional information

Windows-specific - the same files under Docker Linux (oven/bun:canary-slim) correctly pick up new .env values every run.
The transpilation cache lives in %TEMP%\bun-*. Deleting these directories clears the stale cache (but affects all Bun projects).
Workaround: touch every .ts file that reads process.env after any .env change to force re-transpilation.
Any process.env access is affected; import { SQL } from 'bun' in the original project was coincidental.

Why this is HIGH severity:

Silent correctness failure - no error, crash, or log; the application just uses wrong config.
Security risk - rotating compromised credentials in .env has no effect; the old keys remain in the cache.
Operational risk - changing DATABASE_HOST from a dead server to a live one is silently ignored.

What steps can reproduce the bug?
tls.createServer({ requestCert: true }) with rejectUnauthorized left unset is supposed to default to true and reject clients whose certificate can't be verified — that's what PR #31322 fixed. The default is computed by rejectUnauthorizedDefault() in src/js/node/tls.ts, which reads process.env.NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED. That env var is only supposed to affect the client side (whether you accept a remote server's cert when connecting out). On real Node.js it has no effect on a server's own client-cert enforcement. b:
What happened
opencode 1.18.4 (a Bun 1.3.14 standalone executable, NAPI module loaded) segfaults when its
host terminal is rapidly resized down to extreme sizes (~2 cols × 1 row). The crash is inside
the VM's microtask machinery, not application JS — the VM should surface a catchable error
(e.g. RangeError on stack exhaustion) rather than segfault.
Crash reports (two independent hits, same stack family)

https://bun.report/1.3.14/Ma10d9b296mwGugogC________urh5kDunr21Cusw11C+/y34C+qy34C+5sy6Cu657H__urh5kD27p5tC+xt2yCA2K4/vshtD
https://bun.report/1.3.14/Ma10d9b296mwGugogC_______2lkjlDurh5kDunr21Cusw11C+/y34C+qy34C+5sy6Cu657H__urh5kD27p5tC+xt2yCA2K4/ny3zD

Decoded (first report): Segmentation fault at 0x5084EEFFC —
llint_call_javascript → MicrotaskCall::tryCallWithArguments<JSGenerator…> →
callMicrotask (JSMicrotask.cpp:143) → runInternalMicrotask → MicrotaskQueue::drainImpl<true>
→ VM::drainMicrotasks → Bun::jsFunctionDrainMicrotaskQueue (BunProcess.cpp:3806).
Features: spawn, standalone_executable, workers_spawned, napi_module_register, process_dlopen.
Environment
macOS 15 (Darwin 25.4.0), Apple Silicon. The terminal host is xterm.js inside a Tauri app
(PTY via portable-pty); the process group receives SIGWINCH + TIOCSWINSZ per resize step,
~10–120 ms apart, down to 2×1. Process RSS was ~1.0 GB at the time (this instance's normal
baseline in that workspace — not a leak ramp).
Reproduction honesty
Hit twice in the real app (both reports above). We could NOT isolate a standalone repro:
headless PTY harnesses (single jump to 1×1, 1-col staircase drags at 20–100 ms cadence with
bounces, floor jitter, DSR/XTWINOPS query replies, SGR mouse-motion floods with out-of-range
coordinates) all survive. Whatever the missing ingredient is, it's timing/state-dependent in
the real xterm.js byte stream. Happy to run instrumented builds or gather more data.
Downstream mitigation (for anyone else hitting this)
Host-side: never report a grid below 20×5 to the PTY (real terminals have window minimums;
after flooring, the crash class is unreachable). Implemented in our terminal host.

`--max-old-space-size` and JSC heap-cap options are silently ignored — no way to bound the heap, so memory-limited containers OOM where Node completes
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1+9f4682d2a (also reproduced on 1.3.14 stable)
What platform is your computer?
Docker linux/arm64 (oven/bun:canary, oven/bun:1), Apple Silicon host
What steps can reproduce the bug?
--max-old-space-size is accepted by Bun but has no observable effect on heap limiting. The same one-liner on Node aborts at the limit; Bun sails past it and exits 0:
# Node 24: aborts with "JavaScript heap out of memory" at ~256MB (expected)
docker run --rm node:24-slim node --max-old-space-size=256 -e \
  'const a=[];let mb=0;for(;;){a.push(new Array(131072).fill(mb));if(++mb>=600)break};console.log("reached "+mb+"MB")'

# Bun 1.4 canary AND 1.3.14: prints "reached 600MB", exit 0
docker run --rm oven/bun:canary bun --max-old-space-size=256 -e \
  'const a=[];let mb=0;for(;;){a.push(new Array(131072).fill(mb));if(++mb>=600)break};console.log("reached "+mb+"MB")'
The JSC option that should be a hard cap is also accepted but not enforced:
# gcMaxHeapSize parses (an invalid name errors out, this one doesn't) but 600MB allocates fine under a 256MB "cap"
docker run --rm -e BUN_JSC_gcMaxHeapSize=268435456 oven/bun:canary bun -e \
  'const a=[];let mb=0;for(;;){a.push(new Array(131072).fill(mb));if(++mb>=600)break};console.log("reached "+mb+"MB")'
BUN_JSC_forceRAMSize (the recommended equivalent per #6548) and --smol do change GC behavior but neither bounds the heap.
What is the expected behavior?
Either of:

--max-old-space-size=N (already accepted for Node compat) actually constrains the JSC heap — enforce a limit à la gcMaxHeapSize, and/or feed N into the heap-growth policy the way forceRAMSize feeds RAM detection, so the GC works hard before the cgroup kills the process; or
Bun rejects/warns on the flag instead of silently swallowing it, and documents a working alternative.

Cgroup v2 awareness (/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max as the default RAM size for heap heuristics) would fix the container case with zero flags.
What do you see instead?
The flag is silently ignored, and in memory-limited containers that turns into OOM kills for workloads Node completes reliably.
Concrete measurements from an incremental-view-maintenance benchmark (@tanstack/db-ivm; ~600–700MB live working set under heavy allocation churn; identical bench.mjs, docker run --cpus=1 --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g, checksum-verified output):

t: fs.writeFile does not flush on close with O_APPEND, causing data loss on crash
b:
Thank you for submitting a bug report. It helps make Bun better.
What version of Bun is running?
(not provided — please run bun --revision and paste here)
What platform is your computer?
(not provided — please run uname -mprs (macOS/Linux) and paste here)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
When a file is opened with O_APPEND and written via fs.writeFile (or the equivalent write path), Bun does not flush the buffer to disk on close. If the process crashes (or is killed) before the OS would otherwise flush the write, the appended data is lost.
Minimal reproduction pattern:
import { writeFile, openSync, O_APPEND } from "fs";
// open file with O_APPEND, write, then simulate crash before natural flush
// observe appended bytes are missing from the file on restart
A concrete minimal reproduction (GitHub repo / Replit / CodeSandbox) will be added by the reporter — see "Additional information".
What is the expected behavior?
When a file opened with O_APPEND is closed, any buffered writes should be flushed to the underlying file descriptor so that data is durable on close (matching Node.js fs semantics, where close() drains the buffer). A crash after close() returns must not lose the appended data.
What do you see instead?
The appended data is missing from the file after a crash that occurs between the writeFile/write call returning and the OS flushing the buffer. The close path does not issue an explicit flush, so the bytes are lost on abrupt termination.
Additional information
Reported by a user: "Bun's fs.writeFile doesn't flush on close when the file is opened with O_APPEND, causing data loss on crash."
Reporter to follow up with:

bun --revision output
uname -mprs (or Windows equivalent) output
A minimal reproduction link (GitHub repo, Replit, or CodeSandbox)

t: fs.writeFile does not flush on close when file is opened with O_APPEND, causing data loss on crash
b:
Summary
Bun.fs.writeFile does not flush pending writes to disk on close when the destination file is opened with O_APPEND. If the process crashes (or is killed) shortly after the write completes, the appended data is lost — it never reaches the kernel page cache in a durable state before the file descriptor is released.
Steps to Reproduce

Open or create a file with O_APPEND (e.g. a log file that is repeatedly appended to).
Call fs.writeFile(fd, data) (or fs.appendFile) where fd was opened with O_APPEND.
Immediately after the promise resolves, kill the process (kill -9) or trigger a crash.
Reopen the file and inspect its contents.

import { open, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const fh = await open("/tmp/append-test.log", "a"); // O_APPEND
await writeFile(fh, "this line should be durable after close\n");
// Simulate crash before next event loop tick:
process.kill(process.pid, "SIGKILL");
Expected Behavior
On close, any buffered/queued writes for the O_APPEND descriptor should be flushed (via fsync or at minimum fdatasync before the descriptor is released). Data written before close should survive a crash that happens after the writeFile promise has resolved.
Node.js fs.writeFile / fs.appendFile flush on close for descriptors opened with O_APPEND, so appended data is durable once the promise resolves.
Actual Behavior
On Bun, the writeFile promise resolves but the data is not flushed to disk before the descriptor is closed. A crash (or SIGKILL) that happens immediately after the promise resolves loses the appended data. The bytes never appear in the file after recovery.
Environment

Bun version: (please fill in — observed on latest stable as of report date)
OS: Linux
Platform: x86_64

Additional Context
This manifests most visibly for log files opened once with O_APPEND and written to repeatedly. The close path appears to skip the flush that Node performs, so any in-flight pages are dropped on crash rather than being written back before the descriptor is released.
A git bisect was not performed; the behavior appears to be longstanding rather than a regression in a specific release.

t: Advanced IPC and v8.serialize lose Buffer identity (no host-object hook in serializer)
b:
child_process with serialization: 'advanced' and v8.serialize/deserialize round-trip Buffer values as plain Uint8Array — the prototype is lost.
Repro (advanced IPC): fork a child with serialization: 'advanced', cp.send({buffer: Buffer.from('Hello!')}), echo it back: the received value's buffer is a Uint8Array, not a Buffer. Node preserves the Buffer via ChildProcessSerializer._writeHostObject (lib/internal/child_process/serialization.js).
Root cause: both paths go through JSC's SerializedScriptValue, which has no host-object hook, so there is no way to tag Buffer (or other typed-array subclasses) on the wire. A sound fix needs a serializer extension in the WebKit fork or a V8-wire-format serializer implementation.
Currently surfaced by vendored test/js/node/test/parallel/test-child-process-advanced-serialization.js (gated in expectations.txt on the branch that vendored it, citing this gap). Note the test's failure was itself masked on most lanes by the swallowed-rejection bug filed separately.

t: bun test swallows unhandled rejections from a script file's async IIFE
b:
While running vendored Node tests (plain script files, no test() registrations) under bun test --config=bunfig.node-test.toml, an unhandled rejection inside the file's top-level async IIFE does not fail the run.
Concrete case: test/js/node/test/parallel/test-child-process-advanced-serialization.js has a deterministic assertion failure at line 41 (Buffer identity through advanced IPC), yet bun test reported the file as passing on every non-ASAN lane — only the ASAN lane surfaced it, via an unrelated abort. Running the same file directly (bun <file>) fails with the assertion as expected.
Impact: any vendored Node test whose body is an async IIFE can silently rot — CI green does not mean the assertions ran and held. This masked a real runtime gap for some time.
Expected: an unhandled rejection between/outside tests should fail the file, matching how uncaught exceptions between tests are already reported.

t: Feature: mmap the bytecode sidecar read-only so pooled processes share one copy
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
PR #29291 (thanks!) makes ESM bytecode sidecars work without --compile, which makes bytecode usable for the pooled-worker pattern: a manager builds one artifact (app.js + app.js.jsc) and N long-lived worker processes each import() it.
In that shape, the sidecar's memory cost is paid N times. The loader reads the .jsc into a private heap buffer per process — nothing is mmap'd, so the kernel can't share pages across the pool, even though every process is reading the same immutable file.
Measured (macOS arm64, PR #29291 binary 1.4.0-canary.1+a4f165aef; ~1.1 MB bundled ESM artifact with TLA + 5.3 MB .jsc; N long-lived processes each await import(artifact) then hold; medians over 3 rounds, variance ≈ 0):



condition
phys_footprint / proc
aggregate (N procs)




bytecode, N=1
26.0 MB
26.0 MB


bytecode, N=8
26.0 MB
208.0 MB


plain, N=1
21.0 MB
21.0 MB


plain, N=8
21.0 MB
168.0 MB




Cost is perfectly linear: +5 MB phys_footprint per worker, ~the sidecar size, with zero cross-process sharing.
vmmap confirms the mechanism: neither the artifact nor the .jsc appears as a mapped file in any worker (only ICU/tz/plist system files are mapped). The delta shows up as private dirty anonymous memory (SM=PRV): the allocator heap region (mimalloc — Bun's global allocator — tags its anonymous mappings with a VM tag that vmmap displays as IOAccelerator) carries 8256 KB dirty with bytecode vs 2896 KB plain — +5360 KB, almost exactly the 5330 KB sidecar, consistent with the sidecar bytes living in one owned heap allocation per process.
Full raw data and methodology are in the two comments on the PR thread: validation + timing and memory measurement.

robobun confirmed this reading at the source level on that thread:

the sidecar path does a plain File::read_from into an owned buffer (the .jsc branch in src/bundler/transpiler.rs) and transfers ownership to JSC's CachedBytecode, so each process carries a private copy... Nothing in the current loader mmaps the artifact or the sidecar.

and suggested filing this as its own feature request, since it changes the CachedBytecode ownership model rather than the gate removed in #29291.
Where the copy happens today (bun main @ 9f4682d):

src/bundler/transpiler.rs ~L1786: bun_sys::File::read_from(dir, zpath) → contents.into_boxed_slice() → AlreadyBundled::Bytecode(Box<[u8]>) (owned heap buffer).
src/jsc/bindings/ZigSourceProvider.cpp ~L117–L141: that buffer is wrapped via JSC::CachedBytecode

b:
What version of Bun is running?

What platform is your computer?
Linux x64
What steps will reproduce the bug?
This is the client side of a STARTTLS-style mid-connection TLS upgrade, using Bun's low-level raw socket API — Bun.connect() followed by socket.upgradeTLS({ tls: {...}, socket: {...} }) on the resulting plaintext socket. This is not the Node tls compat layer covered by #33924/#33925 (those are server-side and about a different constructor, new tls.TLSSocket(socket, { isServer: true }), verifying an inbound client certificate). This report is about a Bun-native client verifying an inbound server certificate — exactly the shape an SMTP/IMAP client uses for STARTTLS on port 587/143.
tls.rejectUnauthorized: true (and an explicit tls.serverName) is documented as pinning certificate verification. In practice, passing it via upgradeTLS() has no observable effect: a self-signed certificate for the correct hostname, presented in place of one properly signed by a CA the client explicitly trusts, is accepted every time, regardless of rejectUnauthorized's value.
socket.authorized (the Node-compat property inspectable in open()) is not a safe fallback either — it reports true for the same untrusted self-signed certificate, so there's no reliable signal an application can check itself, unlike the server-side case in #33924 where authorized at least came back correctly false.
How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?
Deterministic, 100% reproducible across three separate runs of the PoC below (six sub-cases each run, 18 data points total, byte-for-byte identical each time). Not a race condition — every sub-case settles synchronously in the open()/error() handler on the first and only handshake attempt.
What is the expected behavior?
With rejectUnauthorized: true and an explicit ca naming the one CA the client trusts, a self-signed certificate for the same hostname — signed by nobody, let alone that CA — should be rejected: upgradeTLS()'s socket should fire error/close, never open, the same way tls.connect() (the Node-compat client path) already correctly rejects this exact scenario per the fix in #33846.
What do you see instead?

Native `Bun.InlineWasm` — The DX Holy Grail for Zero-Copy, Sandboxed TS-to-WASM Compilation
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
The entire web and cloud-native ecosystem is betting heavily on WebAssembly (WASM). However, the Developer Experience (DX) for leveraging WASM in modern server-side JavaScript is severely broken and fragmented.
Currently, to achieve C-level performance, developers face two massive hurdles:

Toolchain Hell: They must leave JavaScript, write in a system language (Rust/Zig/C), install external toolchains (Cargo/Emscripten), manually compile .wasm binaries, and write tedious boilerplate to instantiate them via WebAssembly.instantiate. Even using AssemblyScript requires a separate build step and asconfig.json.
The Memory Boundary (IPC) Bottleneck: This is the fatal flaw. Passing complex data (like nested JSON or large arrays) from the JS heap to WASM's linear memory requires expensive serialization, copying, and deserialization (e.g., TextEncoder / TextDecoder). This memory boundary overhead often negates the performance gains of using WASM in the first place.

Bun is built on the philosophy of being an "All-in-One" toolkit. Forcing developers to rely on external build steps and manual memory copying to use WASM fundamentally breaks this philosophy.
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
I propose a paradigm-shifting architecture: integrating a native TS-to-WASM compiler directly into the Bun runtime, featuring Compiler-Magic Memory Sharing (Auto-Memory Hoisting).
By defining a specific block (e.g., namespace Bun.InlineWasm), developers can write a strictly-typed subset of TypeScript directly alongside their normal JS code in the exact same file.
Bun's compiler will hijack this block, bypass the JavaScriptCore engine, and AOT-compile the AST directly into WASM bytecode. More importantly, because Bun controls the compilation, it can perform Auto-Memory Hoisting: when a complex object is passed from the normal TS scope into the InlineWasm scope, Bun automatically allocates that object directly inside the WASM linear memory (or utilizes WasmGC), providing a transparent Proxy to the JS side.
Result: True zero-copy memory sharing with zero developer configuration.

  // Bun.Struct (from previous proposals) naturally aligns with C-ABI/WASM memory
  export const Vector3D = new Bun.Struct({ x: f64, y: f64,

node-compat: `new URL('/x#y', 'thismessage::/')` parses in node, throws in bun, and the jsonschema npm package depends on the node behavior
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14+0d9b296af
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm
What steps can reproduce the bug?
new URL('/x#y', 'thismessage::/');
// node 24.18.0 / 26.3.0: thismessage:/x#y
// bun 1.3.14: throws '"/x#y" cannot be parsed as a URL.'
The divergence is narrow. Here is the matrix (same script under both runtimes):
ref        base               node 24/26          bun 1.3.14
'/x#y'     'thismessage::/'   thismessage:/x#y    THROWS   <- the divergence
'/x'       'thismessage::/'   THROWS              THROWS
'x'        'thismessage::/'   THROWS              THROWS
'#y'       'thismessage::/'   thismessage::/#y    thismessage::/#y
'/x'       'thismessage:/'    thismessage:/x      thismessage:/x
'/x'       'a::/'             THROWS              THROWS
'/x'       'a:/b:/'           a:/x                a:/x

So both runtimes reject a path-absolute ref against an opaque-path base, which is what the WHATWG spec prescribes, except node makes an exception when the ref carries a fragment. Bun rejects that case too.
What is the expected behavior?
Whatever node does, because npm packages depend on it. The jsonschema package's ref resolver does exactly this (https://github.com/tdegrunt/jsonschema/blob/master/lib/validator.js, in Validator.prototype.resolve):
let parsed = new URL(switchSchema, 'thismessage::/');
with switchSchema values like /undefined#/definitions/CommandMetaData. On node that parses and only parsed.hash is consumed. On bun it throws, which in my case took down every CLI command of @adonisjs/ace (it validates command metadata through jsonschema).
What do you see instead?
"/x#y" cannot be parsed as a URL.
Additional information
Reading the URL standard, bun's rejection looks more spec-consistent than node's acceptance: a base with an opaque path should only accept empty or fragment-only relative refs, and node itself rejects /x without the fragment. The fragment exception looks like an Ada quirk. I am filing here first because bun's stated goal is node compatibility and this breaks published packages; happy to take it to Ada/node or jsonschema instead if you consider this a wontfix.
Workaround for anyone else hitting this through jsonschema: patch the base string to 'thismessage:/' (single colon). Both runtimes parse that, and the resolver only reads .hash off the result, which is identical.

t: bun:sqlite: concurrent `new Database(path)` across Workers intermittently sees an empty schema ("no such table")
Runtime transpiler cache causes unknown-extension ESM imports to use the TSX loader on a warm cache
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1+8adb8de8b
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm
What steps can reproduce the bug?
An entry point eligible for Bun's runtime transpiler cache imports an SVG correctly on the first run, but the identical second run incorrectly parses the SVG as TSX.
The entry point must be larger than the cache's 4 KiB minimum. The imported asset itself can be tiny.
mkdir bun-runtime-cache-repro
cd bun-runtime-cache-repro

printf '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"/>' > asset.svg

bun -e 'await Bun.write("run.ts", `import asset from "./asset.svg";\n/*${"x".repeat(5000)}*/\nconsole.log(asset);\n`)'

export BUN_RUNTIME_TRANSPILER_CACHE_PATH="$(mktemp -d)"

bun run run.ts
bun run run.ts
No plugin, mock, or test runner is involved. Setting BUN_RUNTIME_TRANSPILER_CACHE_PATH=0 also makes repeated runs succeed.
What is the expected behavior?
Both invocations should behave identically and print the absolute path to asset.svg, as specified by Bun's built-in file loader:
/path/to/bun-runtime-cache-repro/asset.svg

What do you see instead?
The first invocation succeeds and prints the SVG path.
The identical second invocation, using the now-warm runtime transpiler cache, fails:
SyntaxError: Missing 'default' export in module '/path/to/bun-runtime-cache-repro/asset.svg'.

Bun appears to parse the SVG as TSX on the cache-hit run instead of applying the built-in file loader.
Additional information
This reproduces deterministically on:

1.4.0-canary.1+8adb8de8b
1.4.0-canary.1+dc5748f36
1.4.0-canary.1+aca54d5c2
Darwin arm64 and Linux x64

It was originally observed in a real bun test CI suite. With a fresh explicit cache, the test file passed all 26 tests on the first invocation. The identical second invocation failed while importing an SVG with the same missing-default-export error.
The likely cause is that the runtime-transpiler-cache hit returns before the main module sets has_loaded. Subsequent unknown-extension ESM imports therefore take the entry-point fallback and select the TSX loader instead of the file loader.

t: Async-thrown Error loses its message from error.stack when GC runs before first .stack access
b:
What version of Bun is running?
Reproduced on 1.2.22 and 1.3.14 (latest at time of filing)
What platform is your computer?
Darwin arm64 (macOS 25.0.0, Apple Silicon)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
// repro.mjs
async function boom() { throw new Error("the message"); }
try {
  await boom();
} catch (e) {
  Bun.gc(true); // any GC between construction and first .stack access — organic idle GC triggers it too
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ message: e.message, stackHead: e.stack.split("\n")[0] }));
}
$ bun repro.mjs
{"message":"the message","stackHead":"Error"}

e.message is intact, but the first line of e.stack is a bare Error — the message never makes it into the materialized stack string.
What is the expected behavior?

which is what Node 22 prints for the same script (with globalThis.gc via --expose-gc, or with the timer variant below).
What do you see instead?
stackHead is "Error" — the message is dropped from the stack string.
Additional information
Boundary conditions, all verified on both 1.2.22 and 1.3.14:



Variant
Result




Async-thrown (rejection crosses an await), GC before first .stack read
message lost


Sync-thrown, same forced GC
correct


Async-thrown, await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10)) before read (no forced GC — organic idle GC)
message lost


Async-thrown, setTimeout(…, 0) or a microtask (await Promise.resolve()) before read
correct (loop never idles long enough to GC)


Async-thrown, .stack touched once before the GC (primes materialization), read again after
correct



So the trigger is: an error whose rejection crossed an await boundary, plus any GC before the lazy stack string is first materialized. It looks like whatever pre-materialization data backs the message portion of the deferred stack string is not protected from collection on the async path (the sync path is fine). Possibly adjacent to earlier GC-during-stack-materialization fixes (#25096, #31789), but those were crashes — this is silent data loss.
Real-world impact: we hit this in a compiled CLI (bun build --compile) where errors are formatted via err.stack at top level after async command dispatch — under normal GC pressure roughly 1 in 4 invocations printed error output with no message at all (Command failed, Error\n    at …), which made a user-facing auth hint vanish. t: fetch() connection-refused error shape differs from Node: no e.cause.code === 'ECONNREFUSED'
b:
What
When fetch() fails because the connection is refused, Bun and Node.js expose the failure through different error shapes, which breaks cross-runtime error handling.

Node.js: err.cause.code === 'ECONNREFUSED' (the code is nested on .cause).
Bun: err.code === 'ConnectionRefused' (top-level .code; .cause is undefined).

Code that follows the documented Node/undici shape (if (err.cause?.code === 'ECONNREFUSED')) silently never matches under Bun, so a friendly, actionable error message degrades to a raw "Unable to connect. Is the computer able to access the url?".
Reproduce (Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64)
try {
  await fetch('http://localhost:1/', { method: 'POST' })
} catch (e) {
  console.log('name:', e.name)              // Error
  console.log('message:', e.message)        // "Unable to connect. Is the computer able to access the url?"
  console.log('code:', e.code)              // "ConnectionRefused"
  console.log('cause?.code:', e.cause?.code) // undefined
}
Node prints cause?.code: ECONNREFUSED and no top-level .code for the same call.
Why it matters
Libraries that want a portable "is this a connection-refused error?" check must special-case Bun:
const isConnectionRefused = e =>
  e?.cause?.code === 'ECONNREFUSED' ||   // Node
  e?.code === 'ConnectionRefused'         // Bun
Ask
Align Bun's fetch connection-error shape with Node/undici — ideally exposing the standard ECONNREFUSED-style code on err.cause.code (and the other E* codes: ECONNRESET, ENOTFOUND, ETIMEDOUT, etc.) — or document the Bun shape as intentional so libraries know to check both. Consistency (or documentation) is the fix; either resolves the workaround.
Found while writing cross-runtime tests for a TypeScript toolchain (tjs-lang) whose LLM client runs under both Bun and Node.

COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public

So >640 MB of RSS is unaccounted for by the JS heap — it's native/allocator memory that is never returned. smaps_rollup confirms it is essentially all Private_Dirty/Anonymous (659,516 kB), i.e. not file-backed or shared, not reclaimable by the kernel.

t: AsyncLocalStorage context is lost inside a thenable's then() when the thenable is returned from an async function after an await
`Headers.prototype.clear()` for reusing instances without reallocation
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
Server frameworks that reuse a Headers instance across request cycles (e.g. resetting response headers between requests) currently have no way to clear all headers without allocating a new Headers object. The workaround — iterating .keys() and calling .delete(key) — is slower than allocating a new Headers, leaving allocation as the only performant option.
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
Add Headers.prototype.clear() to remove all header entries in-place, matching the existing API of Map.prototype.clear(), Set.prototype.clear(). This allows reusing the same Headers instance across request cycles without allocating a new one:
headers.clear();
This is a natural extension for a key-value collection type — all other built-in collection types (Map, Set) already have clear().
What alternatives have you considered?


Iterate .keys() and .delete() each header — works but is slower than new Headers() due to JS iterator overhead and per-key hash lookups. Not a viable optimisation.


Reassign = new Headers() — the current approach. Allocates a new internal hash table every request, which shows up as 25%+ of CPU time under load. Wastes memory and GC cycles.


Track dirty keys and delete only those — adds complexity and bookkeeping overhead that negates the benefit for the small number of headers per request (typically 2-5).


Accept the status quo — Headers is not specified to have clear(), so the question is whether a pragmatic non-standard extension is justified. We believe the precedent of Map.clear(), Set.clear() — all designed by the same Web IDL committee — makes this a natural addition that aligns with existing conventions.



Supporting Data
From CPU profiling a Bun server handling ~16k requests:

new Headers(): 25.2% of total runtime (17.29s out of 68.39s)
Iteration workaround (.keys() → .delete()): slower than new Headers() due to JS iterator overhead and per-key hash lookups
A native clear() method would zero the internal hash table in one shot — no allocation, no per-key iteration

What steps can reproduce the bug?

— 265 characters, over the classic Win32 MAX_PATH (260).
Windows long-path support is enabled at the OS level (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem\LongPathsEnabled = 1), and other bun subsystems handle long paths fine (per #21244), but this particular scan still fails.
What is the expected behavior?
bun pm trust <names> / bun pm trust --all and bun pm untrusted should either list the untrusted packages/dependencies with pending lifecycle scripts, or print a normal, mapped error.
What do you see instead?
$ bun pm untrusted
bun pm untrusted v1.3.14 (0d9b296a)

error: An internal error occurred (EUNKNOWN)

From the repo root and from a workspace subdirectory (apps/app) — same monorepo, same node_modules.
With bun --verbose pm untrusted — no additional detail is printed.
bun pm trust (no args) fails differently first, with error: expected package names(s) or --all, which is correct/expected; the bug is in the underlying scan hit by --all or by pm untrusted.

Additional information
EUNKNOWN in bun generally means an OS/Win32 error code came back that bun's errno-mapping layer doesn't recognize — consistent with a raw CreateFileW/NtCreateFile-style call being made without the \\?\ long-path prefix on a path >260 chars, similar to the pattern already reported in:

#8246 — original Windows long-path report (closed, precursor to #21244)
#21244 — added Windows long-path support (merged 2025-07-21) — evidently not applied to the pm trust/pm untrusted package scanner
#33336 (open) — bun:sqlite VFS skips the \\?\ prefix on CreateFileW, same inconsistency in a different subsystem

import
main
What is the expected behavior?
bun --require dual-preload main.js should use the package's require export condition and print:
require
main

This should not be implemented as an extension heuristic. The --require preload should resolve with require conditions and execute through CommonJS require semantics, while --import should continue using import conditions and the ESM loader.
Node handles these as distinct paths: --require calls Module._preloadModules(), which creates a parent module rooted at process.cwd() and calls parent.require(); --import uses the ESM loader.
What do you see instead?
Bun treats --require, --import, and --preload as the same preload kind.
The CLI parser currently flattens all three flags into one ctx.preloads array:
https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/main/src/runtime/cli/Arguments.rs#L939-L966
The runtime then resolves every entry with ImportKind::Stmt and evaluates it through JSModuleLoader::import_ptr:
https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/main/src/runtime/jsc_hooks.rs#L688-L767
As a result, --require selects the import branch of conditional exports.

t: TestReporter inspector events are silently, permanently lost if the process exits before the debugger thread finishes delivering them
macOS: JIT emits AVX on Macs without it, so a darwin-x64 baseline build SIGILLs once code tiers up
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1 (1e35118), built from main for darwin-x64 --baseline=true
What platform is your computer?
Darwin x86_64 — reproduced on two independent machines (see below)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
This is the second half of the pre-AVX2 Mac problem, and it is distinct from #32511.
#32511 / #32512 cover the startup crash: the shipped bun-darwin-x64-baseline links the Haswell macOS WebKit, whose bmalloc constructors use BMI2, so it SIGILLs before main(). oven-sh/WebKit#290 builds the missing Nehalem macOS WebKit and fixes that.
With that artifact in place, bun starts on a pre-AVX Mac — and then dies as soon as any code tiers up, because JavaScriptCore's JIT emits AVX regardless of the CPU:
./bun --version
# 1.4.0  -> rc=0, starts fine

./bun -e 'let s=0; for(let i=0;i<3e7;i++){s+=Math.sqrt(i)*1.000001;} console.log(s)'
# rc=132 -> SIGILL

BUN_JSC_useJIT=0 ./bun -e '...same loop...'
# rc=0   -> works
What is the expected behavior?
A --baseline darwin build should run on a CPU without AVX.
What do you see instead?
SIGILL once the JIT tiers up. The crash banner states the problem better than I can — bun's own CPU detection is correct, and JSC ignores it:
Bun Canary v1.4.0-canary.1 (1e3511800) macOS x64 (baseline)
macOS v14.6.1
CPU: sse42 popcnt                      <-- no AVX

Additional information
Root cause — Source/JavaScriptCore/assembler/MacroAssemblerX86_64.cpp hardcodes AVX as present on Darwin instead of asking the CPU:
#if OS(DARWIN)
        s_avxCheckState = CPUIDCheckState::Set;   // never checks the CPU
#else
        // CPUID.1:ECX.AVX[28] + OSXSAVE[27] + XCR0[2:1] == 11b
#endif
oven-sh/WebKit#198 fixed exactly this for Linux/Windows and guarded the new code with #if !OS(DARWIN), so Darwin kept the assumption. supportsAVX() then feeds ~10 VEX-emitting codegen sites. -march=nehalem cannot help, because the JIT decides at runtime.
Note AVX2 on Darwin is detected correctly, via sysctlbyname("hw.optional.avx2_0"). Only AVX is assumed — so Sandy/Ivy Bridge Macs (AVX, no AVX2) are unaffected by this one; it hits Macs with no AVX at all.

rc=0
rc=0


JIT-heavy loop
rc=132
rc=132


BUN_JSC_useJIT=0
rc=0
rc=0


opencode --version
rc=132
rc=132



Rosetta 2 reports no AVX, so it reproduces the pre-AVX Mac case on rentable hardware.

t: Runtime transpiler cache inlines process.env dot-reads during Worker-thread imports — later processes execute the first process's env values
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 (macOS, Apple Silicon)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
When a sufficiently large module (over the runtime transpiler disk-cache threshold, ~50KB) is dynamically imported inside a Worker thread, Bun's transpiler inlines process.env.X dot-reads as string literals into the transpiled output — and that output is stored in the shared on-disk runtime transpiler cache (~/Library/Caches/bun/@t@/*.pile), keyed by content only. A second process (or later run) with different environment variables gets a cache hit and executes the first process's env values as compile-time constants.
Repro (3 files):
probe-plugin.ts (must exceed the disk-cache threshold — pad with ~800 comment lines):
const k = ["MY", "TEST", "IDENTITY"].join("_")
export const probe = () =>
  console.log("DOT:", process.env.MY_TEST_IDENTITY, "| DYNAMIC:", process.env[k])
// ... ~800 padding comment lines so the file exceeds the runtime transpiler
// disk-cache threshold ...
w.ts:
const mod = await import("./probe-plugin.ts")
mod.probe()
main.ts:
new Worker(new URL("./w.ts", import.meta.url))
Run twice with different env values (file untouched between runs):
MY_TEST_IDENTITY=FIRST_VALUE bun main.ts
MY_TEST_IDENTITY=SECOND_VALUE bun main.ts
What is the expected behavior?
DOT: FIRST_VALUE | DYNAMIC: FIRST_VALUE
DOT: SECOND_VALUE | DYNAMIC: SECOND_VALUE

process.env reads should reflect the running process's environment.
What do you actually see?
DOT: FIRST_VALUE | DYNAMIC: FIRST_VALUE
DOT: FIRST_VALUE | DYNAMIC: SECOND_VALUE   <-- dot-read is stale (run 1's value)

The second run's dot-read returns the FIRST run's value. Inspecting the cached artifact shows the literal baked into the transpiled code where the source has an env read:
$ strings ~/Library/Caches/bun/@t@/<hash>.pile | grep MY_TEST
# transpiled output contains:  "FIRST_VALUE"  (a literal), env expression absent
Notes:

Only the dot-read (process.env.MY_TEST_IDENTITY) is inlined; a computed-key bracket read (process.env[k]) stays live.

t: macOS: no x64 baseline build — `@oven/bun-darwin-x64-baseline` is byte-identical to the AVX2 default
b:
Summary
There is no baseline build for x64 macOS
@oven/bun-darwin-x64-baseline ships the same binary as @oven/bun-darwin-x64 — the AVX2 (-march=haswell) build.
Linux, by contrast, ships a genuine baseline.
Why it matters
On a pre-AVX2 Mac (Sandy/Ivy Bridge — no AVX2/FMA) that binary crashes, and there is no baseline package to fall back to.
This is the upstream cause of downstream reports like anomalyco/opencode#29039 — opencode's -baseline Mac binary SIGILLs on Ivy Bridge.
Who hits it
Pre-Haswell Intel Macs running a macOS that bun supports. Quoting the reports:
anomalyco/opencode#24876:

macOS: 13.7.4
Machine: Macmini6,2 (Intel Ivy Bridge, 2012)
CPU: x86_64 (supports AVX, but NOT AVX2)

macOS 13.7.4 clears bun's 13.0 deployment target; the CPU has no AVX2. That combination is the gap. Same reporter:

This makes the tool unusable on: Intel Macs pre-Haswell (≈ 2013 and earlier) / Any x86_64 CPU without AVX2 support. These machines are still relatively common in development environments.

anomalyco/opencode#29039:

MacBook Pro, Intel Core i7-3520M @ 2.90GHz
macOS 24.6.0 (Darwin)
sysctl -n hw.optional.avx2_0 returns 0 — no AVX2 support

That reporter independently confirmed the packaging bug straight from the Mach-O header:

otool -h shows cpusubtype 3 (CPU_SUBTYPE_X86_64_H — Haswell) for both

For my part, I run OpenCore Legacy Patcher on my mom's 2013 Intel Mac — current macOS, so it clears the deployment target, and the CPU is the only blocker.
Evidence
Every step is reproducible with curl — no bun internals involved.
1. The two darwin packages ship the same binary.
Download both npm packages and hash the bun binary inside each:
ea2f223e94bb2f4bf3050895113c3cf346438f6fa0501c8532284e063f72f7a0  @oven/bun-darwin-x64@1.3.14
ea2f223e94bb2f4bf3050895113c3cf346438f6fa0501c8532284e063f72f7a0  @oven/bun-darwin-x64-baseline@1.3.14

Identical hash, identical 69,173,328 bytes — byte-for-byte the same file. The "baseline" package is not a distinct build.
2. That binary is the AVX2 build.
Disassembling it (Mach-O, x86_64) finds 248,019 AVX2 (ymm) + 7,049 AVX-512 (zmm) instructions — i.e. the modern (-march=haswell) build, which a pre-AVX2 CPU can't run.
3. Linux ships a real baseline; darwin doesn't.
Same comparison on the linux packages — default and baseline are different binaries:
9fd36f87e4b90b07632b987a2e4ec81ca15a62c81bf983190cea6d715be2ad74  @oven/bun-linux-x64@1.3.14
a8f9ebd1770ddc8e55dab7a68d4ec1ec1eebf374bb97cc65cf2c3cb373fc6791  @oven/bun-linux-x64-baseline

t: Bun Shell: stdout/stderr are relayed via pipes, not inherited — add explicit `inherit` option or make default truly inherit
b:
Summary
Bun.$ is documented as inheriting the parent process's stdout/stderr/stdin, but in practice only stdin is a real TTY — stdout and stderr are pipes that Bun relays to the parent. As a result, spawned commands see isatty(1) === false and disable colors / progress bars / pagers.
Reproduction
// run from a real terminal
await Bun.$`python3 -c "import sys;print(sys.stdin.isatty(),sys.stdout.isatty(),sys.stderr.isatty())"`;
// -> True False False
Same finding as #33234.
Impact
Any command that checks isatty(1) degrades: ls/git drop colors, cargo loses its progress bar, pagers behave like cat. The core color issue #11046 (open since 2024-05) traces back to this. Today the only shell-level workaround is .env({ FORCE_COLOR: "3" }), which depends on every child supporting FORCE_COLOR (tsc, composer, etc. don't).
What's missing
There's no escape hatch on ShellPromise to make stdout/stderr a real inherited fd:
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.getPrototypeOf(Bun.$`true`))
// constructor cwd env quiet nothrow throws text json lines arrayBuffer bytes blob run then
#10515 requested .inheritStdio() and was closed with "by default the shell will use stdout, stderr, and stdin of the bun process" — but the reproduction above shows that's not the case for stdout/stderr; they're pipes, not inherited fds.
Proposal
Either (or both):


Add an explicit inherit option, e.g. .stdout("inherit") / .stderr("inherit") / .inheritStdio(), mirroring Bun.spawn's stdio: "inherit" and zx's stdio API. When set, pass the parent's fd directly to the child so isatty() is true.


Change the default to truly inherit stdout/stderr (only piping when .quiet() / .text() / etc. is used), matching how dax (@david/shell) behaves:


// dax's CommandBuilder default state
#state = {
  stdin: "inherit",
  stdout: { kind: "inherit" },
  stderr: { kind: "inherit" },
  // ...
};
In dax, await $`cmd` keeps colors by default, and only switches to piped when a capture method (.text() / .quiet()) is called. This is why dax has essentially no "colors lost from subprocess" issues, while Bun shell / zx / execa all do.
Why this over the PTY route (#33239)
#33239 adds .terminal(term) (PTY) and is great for full-screen / interactive programs. But the inherit path is valuable on its own:

Cross-platform: PTY (Bun.Terminal) is POSIX-only; fd inheritance works on Windows too.
Lighter: no extra PTY allocation, no data callbacks, no manual close().
Sufficient for the common case: the vast majority of "lost colors" repo

t: fs.watch: per-watcher registration cost grows super-linearly — 5000 watchers take 74s (58ms in Node)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (also reproduced on the latest release)
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 (macOS, Apple Silicon, 14 cores)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
The cost of each individual fs.watch() call grows super-linearly with the number of watchers already registered in the process. In Node it is flat.
This matters because that is exactly what chokidar does: it registers one fs.watch per file. Any dev server built on chokidar (Nuxt, Vite plugins, webpack tooling, …) will register thousands of watchers on a medium/large project.
Self-contained repro (creates its own temp files, no dependencies):
// repro-fswatch.mjs
import { mkdtempSync, writeFileSync, rmSync, watch } from 'node:fs'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'
import { join } from 'node:path'

const runtime = typeof Bun !== 'undefined' ? `bun ${Bun.version}` : `node ${process.version}`

const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'fswatch-bench-'))
const files = []
for (let i = 0; i < 5000; i++) {
  const f = join(dir, `file-${i}.txt`)
  writeFileSync(f, 'x')
  files.push(f)
}

console.log(`[${runtime}] watching ${files.length} files individually (what chokidar does per file)\n`)

const handles = []
let done = 0

for (const mark of [500, 1500, 3000, 5000]) {
  const batch = files.slice(done, mark)
  const t = performance.now()
  for (const f of batch) handles.push(watch(f, () => {}))
  const ms = performance.now() - t
  done = handles.length
  console.log(
    `  watchers: ${String(done).padStart(4)} | this batch of ${String(batch.length).padStart(4)}` +
    ` took ${String(Math.round(ms)).padStart(6)} ms -> ${(ms / batch.length).toFixed(2)} ms per watcher`
  )
}

for (const h of handles) h.close()
rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })
Run it under both runtimes:
node repro-fswatch.mjs
bun  repro-fswatch.mjs

What is the expected behavior?
Registering a watcher should cost roughly the same regardless of how many watchers already exist, as it does in Node:
[node v26.4.0] watching 5000 files individually

  watchers:  500 | this batch of  500 took      6 ms -> 0.01 ms per watcher
  watchers: 1500 | this batch of 1000 took     12 ms -> 0.01 ms per watcher
  watchers: 3000 | this batch of 1500 took     17 ms -> 0.01 ms per watcher
  watchers: 5000 | this batch of 2000 took     23 ms -> 0.01 ms per watcher

Total for 5000 watchers: 58 ms.
What do you see instead?
Per-watcher cost keeps climbing as watchers accumulate — roughly 0.8 ms → 24 ms:
[bun 1.3.14] watchin

t: Windows: uv_run's alive-guard wedges teardown states with zero ref'd handles (server.close() waits forever class)
b:
Mechanism (fully established, A/B-proven on CI agents)
On Windows, Bun drives libuv via tick_with_timeout → uv_run(UV_RUN_ONCE). uv_run's alive-guard (while (r != 0 && ...)) skips both timer processing and I/O polling when the loop has no ref'd handles or active requests. Every uSockets handle (socket polls, asyncs, prepare/check, sweep timer) is uv_unref'd by design — socket liveness is tracked by Bun-side KeepAlives that bump uv's active_handles counter directly.
Consequence: any state where all Bun KeepAlives drop while a socket still awaits an event wedges completely — no I/O delivery, no JS timer can fire (ref'd or unref'd; the JS-timer bridge uv_timer in timer::All::ensure_uv_timer is itself unref'd without ref'd JS timers), until an unrelated ref'd uv handle appears. The epoll/kqueue path has no such gap: us_loop_run_bun_tick polls unconditionally, bounded by Bun's next-JS-timer deadline (which the Windows path discards entirely).
Canonical repro state: node:http server half-closes a connection mid-upload (res.socket.end()), response never end()ed, client aborts; server.close() (graceful stop releases the server's KeepAlive immediately in stop_listening) then awaits a teardown event the loop will never deliver. test-http-should-not-emit-or-throw-error-when-writing-after-socket.end.ts (quarantined-on-main class) times out exactly here; an identical copy with a ref'd 5s interval passes on the same lane in the same build, while an unref'd 15s watchdog never fires during the stall.
Fix attempts on PR #32488 (reverted, with reasons)

us_loop_run_bun_tick for libuv (ref the wakeup async around uv_run, scratch uv_timer for the deadline): unwedged the blocking branch, but making Windows JS timers punctual globally broke tests depending on the historical lazy-timer timing (proxy-tunnel timeouts, test-tls-connect-memleak RSS timing, unconsume/upgrade).
Same bypass in us_loop_pump (the tick_without_idle branch auto_tick takes when is_active() is false — the branch actually hit in the wedge): unwedged the tests, but delivering I/O during legitimate keepalive-zero transition windows (socket handoffs: upgrade, unconsume, proxy CONNECT tunnels) broke those flows.
Keep the server's KeepAlive through a graceful stop until deinit_if_we_can drains (Node parity — server.close() keeps the process alive until connections end): correct in principle, but upgrade-detached connections never decrement pending_requests (pre-existing bookkeeping gap — all_closed_promise silentl

t: Writable.toWeb() breaks when a preload script requires node:stream
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (and current main)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
Writable.toWeb() returns a broken WritableStream when any preload script has required node:stream (or node:zlib).
preload.js:
require("node:stream");
repro.js:
const { Writable } = require("stream");
const w = new Writable({ write(c, e, cb) { cb(); } });
const ws = Writable.toWeb(w);
ws.close().then(
  () => console.log("RESOLVED (wrong)"),
  e => console.log("rejected:", e.code, "(correct)"),
);
w.end();
bun repro.js                      # rejected: ABORT_ERR (correct)
bun --preload ./preload.js repro.js   # RESOLVED (wrong) + TypeError below
node --require ./preload.js repro.js  # rejected: ABORT_ERR (correct)

What is the expected behavior?
Same as without the preload, and same as Node: ending the underlying stream.Writable errors the WritableStream, so ws.close() rejects with ABORT_ERR.
What do you see instead?
ws.close() resolves instead of rejecting, and the end-of-stream callback then throws:
TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'handleKnownInternalErrors')
      at <anonymous> (internal:webstreams_adapters:204:15)
      at <anonymous> (internal:shared:113:35)
      at onclose (internal:streams/end-of-stream:170:21)
      at emit (node:events:142:22)
      at emitCloseNT (internal:streams/destroy:104:14)

handleKnownInternalErrors is a plain function declaration in the same builtin module
(src/js/internal/webstreams_adapters.ts) as its two call sites, so it should never be
undefined. It only becomes undefined when the module is first pulled in from a preload
script, which suggests the builtin's module-scope bindings are not fully initialized on that
path — newWritableStreamFromStreamWritable's eos() callback then faults, and the
closed promise settles the wrong way.
Additional information
Reproduces on released 1.3.14 and on current main (i.e. it predates the C++ web-streams
rewrite in #33193). node:zlib in the preload triggers it too — webstreams_adapters.ts
reads processBindingConstants.zlib at module scope.
Found while porting Node's upstream web-streams tests (#32627): it makes
test/parallel/test-whatwg-webstreams-adapters-to-writablestream.js fail under the
node-test harness, whose preload requires node:stream. That file is left out of the
vendored set until this is fixed.

t: Bun.build renames a function parameter to shadow a referenced global function
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14
What platform is your computer?
macOS 26.5.1 (25F80), arm64
What steps can reproduce the bug?
This file reproduces the bug when bundled with the steps below: https://gist.github.com/theopak/6536127d85204bfc4b1dc7a8dc6890a6#file-bun-symbol-resolution-repro-js
First, run the input directly as a control:
bun bun-symbol-resolution-repro.js
Then bundle and run it:
bun build bun-symbol-resolution-repro.js --outdir out
bun out/bun-symbol-resolution-repro.js
The failure reproduced in three consecutive clean runs.
What is the expected behavior?
Bundling valid JavaScript should preserve its symbol bindings.
The input contains the equivalent of:
async function J7A(A, B, Q) {
  const result = A3(B.projectId, null);
}
A3 is a global function. The parameter A and global A3 are different symbols.
What do you see instead?
Bun renames the parameter A to A3, shadowing the referenced global function:
async function J7A(A3, B, Q) {
  const result = A3(B.projectId, null);
}
The bundled output then fails:
TypeError: A3 is not a function.
(In 'A3(g, null)', 'A3' is an instance of Object)
    at J7A

Directly running the input does not produce this collision.
This is a severe correctness failure because a successful production build can silently change valid program semantics and ship type-confused runtime crashes in code that worked before bundling.
Additional information
This requires only one entrypoint and a normal bun build. Compilation and bytecode generation are not involved.
The fixture is intentionally large because the failure depends on the scope graph and identifier-renaming order. Removing unrelated scopes can change the assigned names and make the failure disappear. The core problem is that the identifier renamer assigns a function parameter the same name as a referenced global, changing program semantics.
AI Disclosure: Repro case and issue text created by GPT-5.6-Sol and reviewed by me.

4A17CD88-9E15-3FED-B870-A9FE3ED3C3C8, so symbols and line numbers are exact)

What steps can reproduce the bug?
We can reproduce it reliably, but only in a real-world-sized workload so far:

bun test --parallel over a suite of 326 files / ~2,100 tests in which many tests exercise code that calls
node:child_process.execFileSync("git", [...]) (bun routes this through Bun.spawnSync →
spawnMaybeSync). The same worker processes also run in-process HTTP servers (Bun.serve + fetch), SSE
streams, timers, async Bun.spawns, and bun:sqlite — i.e. lots of fd churn around the sync spawns.
On an idle machine, ~1 in 5 full-suite runs never finishes: suite output stops, the coordinator goes
idle, and one or more --test-worker processes peg a core at ~100 % CPU forever. Two workers wedged
simultaneously in one observed run.
Worker parallelism is not required: the same suite run serially (bun test --isolate, no --parallel,
single process, files one-at-a-time) wedged the same way with the same stack. The probability appears to
scale with the number of spawnSync calls, not with concurrency.

being missed).
What we could NOT do: distill it to a standalone snippet. A synthetic 12-file suite doing 2,400 bare
execFileSync("git", ["--version"]) calls per run produced zero wedges in 40 runs (~96 k spawns). The
trigger seems to need the surrounding event-loop/fd activity, which is why we suspect stale poll or
fd-recycling state on the per-VM singleton SpawnSyncEventLoop kqueue. We're happy to run instrumented
builds or additional diagnostics against the real workload.

spawnSync returns when the child exits. Worst case — if the runtime somehow misses the exit — the

At wedge time the worker always has exactly one child, and it is a zombie — the child exited, bun never

SIGTRAP: C++ exception in __cxa_finalize_ranges at exit after in-process onnxruntime (via @huggingface/transformers) inference — tests pass, teardown panics
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.10 (30e609e)
What platform is your computer?
macOS 26.5.1 arm64 (Apple Silicon)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
Run real ONNX inference in-process via @huggingface/transformers (which dlopens libonnxruntime.1.21.0.dylib through onnxruntime-node), let the tests/script complete, and let the process exit normally.
// bun test repro shape — any test that does real in-process ONNX inference:
import { pipeline } from "@huggingface/transformers";
const embed = await pipeline("feature-extraction", "jinaai/jina-embeddings-v3");
await embed("hello world");
// ... all assertions pass ...
// crash fires AFTER results are printed, during process exit
Observed consistently (3/3 standalone runs, 40+ identical crash reports over 5 days): the test file prints 11 pass / 0 fail ... Ran 11 tests, then panic(main thread): A C++ exception occurred / oh no: Bun has crashed with SIGTRAP. Any bun test set that includes the ONNX-exercising file crashes; the same set without it exits 0. Bisection ruled out co-resident native modules (sqlite-vec vec0.dylib, sharp libvips-cpp, homebrew libsqlite3) — each is clean alone and in pairs; only the onnxruntime-exercising file triggers it.
What is the expected behavior?
Process exits 0 after tests pass.
What happens instead?
SIGTRAP (EXC_BREAKPOINT) on the main thread inside C++ static-destructor finalization at exit:
libc++abi.dylib   std::__terminate(void (*)())
libc++abi.dylib   std::terminate()
libsystem_c.dylib __cxa_finalize_ranges
libsystem_c.dylib exit
bun               (atexit/main teardown)

ONNX Runtime registers C++ global/static destructors + background thread pools; after real inference has run, one of those destructors throws in a noexcept teardown context during __cxa_finalize_ranges → std::terminate() → SIGTRAP. Bun's own crash line notes napi_module_register process_dlopen(2) exited — a dlopen'd napi module, panic at exit.
bun.report (redacted stack from the live repro):
https://bun.report/1.3.10/Mt130e609egjmQgwggCm3629C2stx+Cm6v6sB____2prB2qhsCmil9Juiz1kBu9m+EmsoqF2hrB+giB
Additional information

The crash is purely at teardown — all test results are final and correct before it fires. Exit code is the only casualty (breaks CI/test-gating on exit codes).
Workaround we ship: shard ONNX-exercising tests and judge them on the printed summary instead of exit code; and route inference out-of-process. A _exit(0)-style skip of static dtors also avoids it, but there's no supported hook in bun t

t: Bun.build() leaks native memory per call (RSS unbounded, heapUsed flat) — kills long-lived watch/dev processes
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (darwin/arm64, Apple Silicon)
What platform is your computer?
Darwin arm64 (macOS)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
Every call to Bun.build() strands native memory that is never returned. RSS grows
without bound across sequential builds, while heapUsed stays completely flat — so it
is invisible to Bun.gc(true) and to any JS heap profiler.
Self-contained repro (no dependencies — it generates its own module graph):
// leak.ts — bun leak.ts [moduleCount] [iterations]
import { mkdirSync, writeFileSync, rmSync } from 'fs'
import { tmpdir } from 'os'
import { join } from 'path'

const MODULES = Number(process.argv[2] ?? 1500)
const ITERS = Number(process.argv[3] ?? 15)

const root = join(tmpdir(), `bun-build-leak-${process.pid}`)
const src = join(root, 'src')
mkdirSync(src, { recursive: true })

for (let i = 0; i < MODULES; i++) {
  writeFileSync(
    join(src, `m${i}.ts`),
    `export const v${i} = (x: number): number => {\n` +
      Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, k) => `  x = (x + ${k}) * 1.0001`).join('\n') +
      `\n  return x + ${i}\n}\n`
  )
}
writeFileSync(
  join(src, 'entry.ts'),
  Array.from({ length: MODULES }, (_, i) => `import { v${i} } from './m${i}'`).join('\n') +
    `\nexport const all = [${Array.from({ length: MODULES }, (_, i) => `v${i}`).join(',')}]\n` +
    `console.log(all.length)\n`
)

const mb = (n: number) => (n / 1e6).toFixed(1).padStart(7)
let base = 0
for (let i = 1; i <= ITERS; i++) {
  const result = await Bun.build({
    entrypoints: [join(src, 'entry.ts')],
    outdir: join(root, 'out'),
    target: 'browser',
    ...(process.env.MINIFY ? { minify: true } : {}),
    ...(process.env.SOURCEMAP ? { sourcemap: 'linked' as const } : {}),
  })
  if (!result.success) { console.error(result.logs); break }
  Bun.gc(true) // force a full GC: anything still held is genuinely retained
  const { rss, heapUsed } = process.memoryUsage()
  if (i === 1) base = rss
  console.log(`build ${String(i).padStart(2)}  rss=${mb(rss)}MB  heapUsed=${mb(heapUsed)}MB  Δrss=${mb(rss - base)}MB`)
}
rmSync(root, { recursive: true, force: true })
bun leak.ts 1500 15                     # +51.6MB over 15 builds
MINIFY=1 SOURCEMAP=1 bun leak.ts 1500 15  # +83.7MB over 15 builds

What is the expected behavior?
Memory used by a completed Bun.build() is released, so a process that bundles
repeatedly (a watch/dev server) has flat RSS across rebuilds.
What do you see instead?
RSS grows monotonically per call and does not plateau.

bun install leaks package-extraction temp directories (.{16hex}-{8digits}.tmp) into $TMPDIR; filled 25 GB on a long-lived CI container
b:
What happens
bun install leaks its package-extraction temp directories into $TMPDIR and never removes them, even when the install exits 0. Each leaked entry is a directory named .{16 hex chars}-{8 digits}.tmp (for example .5dfdff2c5fefbff7-00000006.tmp) containing the extracted contents of an npm package.
On machines where the OS periodically cleans the temp dir this goes unnoticed. On a long-lived container it is fatal: nothing ever cleans /tmp, so the leak grows until the disk fills.
Impact we measured

Linux (Debian-based GitHub Actions runner container, x64): repeated bun install runs in a Bun-workspaces monorepo accumulated ~25 GB of these directories in /tmp over ~40 hours, at ~37 MB per directory, and drove the host disk past 90%. All installs succeeded; the leak is not tied to crashes or failed installs.
macOS (arm64, Bun 1.3.14): same pattern in $TMPDIR. 22 leaked directories currently present, dated across the last three weeks. Example listing:

drwxr-xr-x@  2 marcos staff  64 Jun 22 03:53 .1dba7fff6bf6ffb8-00000002.tmp
drwxr-xr-x@  9 marcos staff 288 Jun 23 03:35 .1dbe8ded7fb73bd2-00000008.tmp
drwxr-xr-x@  9 marcos staff 288 Jul  1 03:35 .3eff58f797b1ad7c-00000002.tmp
drwxr-xr-x@ 15 marcos staff 480 Jul  4 04:13 .5dfdff2c5fefbff7-00000006.tmp

.5dfdff2c5fefbff7-00000006.tmp contains a complete extracted react-native package tree (Libraries/, ReactCommon/, ReactAndroid/, sdks/, ...). On macOS du reports the trees as taking ~0 blocks (presumably clonefile/hardlink from the cache), but on the Linux container each directory held ~37 MB of real data.
What I expected
Temp extraction directories are deleted before bun install returns, or at minimum on the next install.
Environment

Bun 1.3.14 (also observed on earlier 1.3.x)
macOS arm64 and Linux x64 (Debian-based container, ext4, /tmp on the root filesystem)
Plain bun install in a Bun-workspaces monorepo, default cache settings

Notes

My best guess at the mechanism, from the documented extract-then-rename-into-global-cache model: some extraction paths skip the cleanup/rename of the temp directory. That is inference, not verified against source.
Closest existing issue I found is #14793, which is the same class of bug (temp directory left behind, never cleaned) but for bun upgrade rather than bun install.
Our workaround on long-lived containers is a post-job sweep of stale /tmp entries; happy to test a fix or provide more data.
