t: Heap use-after-free: coordination object destroyed/freed while a thread is still waiting on it (deterministic PoC on macOS arm64 + Linux aarch64 musl; + bun.report traces)
Use-after-free: coordination object's pthread_cond/mutex destroyed while a thread is still blocked in pthread_cond_timedwait (latent race)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (aarch64, musl)
What platform is your computer?
ARM64 Linux (aarch64-linux-musl), running under the iSH user-mode emulator on
iOS/macOS. (The crash is timing-sensitive — see "Why it doesn't reproduce on fast
native hardware" below.)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
A workload that runs CPU-bound background worker threads (here: a Rust cdylib
loaded via bun:ffi using rayon/crossbeam) concurrently with heavy JS
allocation (JSC GC churn):
import { dlopen, FFIType } from "bun:ffi";
const lib = dlopen("./libfffw.so", {
  fffw_start:{args:[],returns:FFIType.void},
  fffw_stop:{args:[],returns:FFIType.void},
});
lib.symbols.fffw_start();                 // spins up rayon SIMD workers
for (let r=0;r<2500;r++){ let a=[]; for(let i=0;i<8000;i++) a.push({x:i,y:"s"+i,z:[i]}); }
lib.symbols.fffw_stop();
Crashes ~80–90% of runs during the allocation loop (not at teardown),
"multiple threads are crashing", at a small/garbage address.
What is the expected behavior?
No crash; the program runs to completion.
What do you see instead?
SIGSEGV inside pthread_cond_timedwait's internal waiter-list unlink, writing
through a node pointer that holds a code address (i.e. freed-and-reused
memory). The faulting store is *node_next = node_prev where node_next was read
from a coordination object whose memory has already been freed/zeroed.
Root cause (from disassembly of the crash site)
The crashing thread is in this pattern (a "wait until predicate, then destroy"
coordination object; x19 = the object):
;  while (obj->busy) { cond_timedwait(&obj->cond, &obj->mutex); unlock; lock; }
bl  pthread_cond_timedwait
add x0,x19,#8 ; bl pthread_mutex_unlock
add x0,x19,#8 ; bl pthread_mutex_lock
ldr x8,[x19,#0x60] ; cbnz x8, <loop>          ; obj->busy
add x0,x19,#8 ; bl pthread_mutex_unlock
mov x0,x19    ; bl <dtor>                      ; tear the object down:

<dtor>:
ldr x0,[x19,#0x68]; str xzr,[x19,#0x68]; bl <dtor>   ; (drain a list)
bl  pthread_cond_destroy
bl  pthread_mutex_destroy
; ... free(obj)

The object is destroyed (pthread_cond_destroy + pthread_mutex_destroy) and
freed right after the predicate clears, without proving that every thread
blocked in pthread_cond_timedwait(&obj->cond, …) has actually woken, re-acquired
the mutex, and left the wait. Per POSIX, destroying a condition variable with any
blocked waiter is undefined behavior; a woken-but-not-yet-returned waiter then
dereferences freed memory.

t: scripts/vs-shell.ps1 fails to detect VS BuildTools-only installs (vswhere call omits -products *)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14+0d9b296af
What platform is your computer?
No response
What steps can reproduce the bug?
On a Windows machine where Visual Studio is installed as Build Tools only (no IDE) — e.g. C:\Program Files       (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools — build Bun from source:
bun bd
Comparing vswhere with and without -products * shows the cause:
▎ vswhere -prerelease -latest -property installationPath
▎ (empty)
▎ vswhere -prerelease -latest -products * -property installationPath
▎ C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools
What is the expected behavior?
The build locates the installed VS toolchain (including a Build Tools–only install) and proceeds.
What do you see instead?
The build aborts during environment setup:
Loading Visual Studio environment, this may take a second...
Exception: ...\scripts\vs-shell.ps1:32
throw "Visual Studio directory not found."
Additional information
Root cause
scripts/vs-shell.ps1 detects the install with:
$vsDir = (& $vswhere -prerelease -latest -property installationPath)

vswhere excludes Build Tools by default — it only returns them with -products * (or an explicit -products
Microsoft.VisualStudio.Product.BuildTools). So on a Build Tools–only machine this returns empty, and the fallback    
block then only searches hardcoded ...\2022 directories, missing both Build Tools and non-2022 versions (e.g. VS 18).
The script then throws.

Suggested fix

Add -products * to the vswhere call:

$vsDir = (& $vswhere -prerelease -latest -products * -property installationPath)

(Optionally broaden the hardcoded 2022-only fallback paths, but -products * resolves the primary issue.)

t: bun test: ESM `export *` re-exports unresolved on Linux but not macOS (drizzle-orm: "Export named 'sql' not found")
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (oven-sh/setup-bun@v2 on GitHub Actions; also reproduced via local install)
What platform is your computer?

Fails: Linux x64 (ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions runner)
Works: macOS arm64 (local), same Bun 1.3.14

What steps can reproduce the bug?
A test file (run with bun test) that imports named exports from drizzle-orm@0.45.2:
import { sql, asc, desc, count, lt, lte, inArray } from 'drizzle-orm'
On Linux, bun test fails at module load:
SyntaxError: Export named 'sql' not found in module
'.../node_modules/drizzle-orm/index.js'.
(also 'asc', 'desc', 'count', 'lt', 'lte', 'inArray')

drizzle-orm's ESM entry (index.js, resolved via the import condition) re-exports its public API through chains of export * from "./sql/index.js" (and similar). Bun's loader on Linux does not surface those re-exported names; on macOS (identical Bun version and identical bun.lock) the same imports resolve and the suite passes.
What is the expected behavior?
export * re-export chains resolve identically across platforms, so import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm' works under bun test on Linux as it does on macOS.
Ruled out

Stale install/cache: a clean rm -rf node_modules && bun install --frozen-lockfile on Linux still fails.
Bun version: 1.3.14 is current; an older 1.3.8 fails identically.
NODE_ENV / config: failure is independent of NODE_ENV and bunfig.toml.
Bundler vs loader: the same project's next build (webpack) on the same Linux runner resolves drizzle-orm fine; only Bun's native test-runner loader fails. This points at Bun's ESM export * resolution on Linux rather than the package.

Happy to assemble a minimal standalone reproduction if useful.

t: tls.connect({ socket }) over a Windows named pipe can re-emit post-upgrade bytes on the original socket
b:
Follow-up carved out of #32241 (fix for #32239).
Summary
#32241 stops tls.connect({ socket }) from re-emitting post-upgrade bytes on the original net.Socket for the TCP path (the socket.upgradeTLS() branches in Socket.prototype.connect, guarded via a kupgradedToTLS flag checked in the net.Socket data handlers).
The sibling upgradeDuplexToTLS path is not covered. It is taken when isNamedPipeSocket(socket) is true, i.e. a net.Socket backed by a Windows named pipe (isNamedPipeSocket is always false on POSIX, so this is Windows-only). On that path:

connection._handle is not replaced (unlike the TCP path, which sets connection._handle = raw), so the original native pipe handle keeps firing SocketHandlers2.data with self = connection.
The TLS layer is fed through the connection's public data event (connection.on("data", events[0])).

So post-upgrade bytes reach both the TLS feeder (intended) and any pre-existing user data listener (the STARTTLS re-entry from #32239).
Why the #32241 flag cannot be reused here
Setting connection[kupgradedToTLS] = true in the duplex branches would make the data handler's guard suppress self.push(buffer), which is the only thing producing the data events events[0] consumes. That would starve the TLS feeder and break TLS over named pipes entirely. This path needs a structurally different fix (e.g. have the duplex wrapper consume the connection's reads without going through the user-observable data event, matching how Node takes over the stream).
Scope / platform

Windows named pipes only.
Pre-existing (not introduced by #32241).
Pure Duplex transports also take this branch but do not use SocketHandlers2, so the specific re-emission described here does not apply to them.

Code references: src/js/node/net.ts (the upgradeDuplex branches in Socket.prototype.connect), src/runtime/socket/socket_body.rs (js_upgrade_duplex_to_tls, js_is_named_pipe_socket).

t: jsc.startSamplingProfiler(directory) segfaults: runtime write to frozen JSC::Config
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary (885c44f), also current main. Linux x64.
What steps will reproduce the bug?
// crash.mjs
import jsc from "bun:jsc";
jsc.startSamplingProfiler("/tmp/profdir");
bun crash.mjs segfaults 100% of the time. Calling jsc.startSamplingProfiler() with no directory argument works fine (the profiler starts and jsc.samplingProfilerStackTraces() returns data), so the crash is specific to the directory/report-at-exit path.
panic(main thread): Segmentation fault at address 0x45D4BD8

Root cause
functionStartSamplingProfiler (src/jsc/modules/BunJSCModule.h:459) assigns a JSC option at runtime:
Options::samplingProfilerPath() = pathCString.span().data();
samplingProfiler.registerForReportAtExit();
JSC option storage lives inside g_jscConfig (JSCConfig.h:104, OptionsStorage options;), and the config pages are mprotected read-only by Config::permanentlyFreeze() (WTFConfig.cpp:200) during startup. Any assignment to Options:: after the freeze is a write to a read-only page, hence the deterministic SEGV. ASAN on a debug build confirms:
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV ... The signal is caused by a WRITE memory access.
    #0 functionStartSamplingProfiler(JSC::JSGlobalObject*, JSC::CallFrame*) src/jsc/modules/BunJSCModule.h:459:45

Two adjacent defects at the same site, for whoever picks this up:

pathCString is function-local, so even if the write succeeded, the stored const char* would dangle by the time SamplingProfiler::reportDataToOptionFile() reads it at exit (SamplingProfiler.cpp:1210).
The report mechanism relies on atexit (SamplingProfiler.cpp:1205). Setting the path before the freeze via BUN_JSC_useSamplingProfiler=1 BUN_JSC_samplingProfilerPath=<dir> avoids the crash but still produces no report file on a normal exit, so the atexit route does not appear to fire on Bun's exit path either.

A fix likely needs to bypass the Options + atexit mechanism and keep the path on the Bun side, writing the report during VM/global teardown instead.

t: Rename $zig() JS→native binding macro and decouple it from .zig reference files
b:
Problem
The $zig("foo.zig", "symbol") macro in src/js/ is the JS→native binding mechanism. After the Zig→Rust port:

The name $zig is misleading — the implementations are in Rust (src/sql_jsc/mysql.rs:3 create_binding, etc.).
The first argument ("mysql.zig") is used by src/codegen/generate-js2native.ts as a path key: resolveNativeFileId() scans src/ for .zig files and requires the named .zig file to exist on disk or throws "Could not find file <name>.zig in $zig call". The resolved path becomes part of the mangled C symbol (JS2Zig___src_sql_jsc_mysql_zig__createBinding).
CLAUDE.md says the .zig siblings "are not compiled and not where new code goes" — but they are load-bearing for codegen path resolution. Deleting them as dead code breaks the build.

24 $zig() call sites across src/js/ (net, tls, zlib, crypto, os, sql, internal-for-testing, assert/myers_diff).
Proposed fix

Rename the macro $zig → $native (and $newZigFunction → $newNativeFunction) in src/codegen/replacements.ts and src/codegen/generate-js2native.ts.
Make resolveNativeFileId accept .rs filenames (or drop the file-existence check and treat the first arg as a plain namespace string), so the .zig reference files are no longer required for the build to succeed.
Update all 24 call sites in src/js/ to the new name and .rs (or bare) key.
Update the mangled symbol scheme in the generated header + the Rust #[no_mangle] exports to match (or keep the existing mangled names via a compat table so this is JS-side-only).
Update CLAUDE.md to drop the implicit "you can delete .zig files" hazard once they are truly unreferenced.

Files

src/codegen/generate-js2native.ts (the macro impl + resolveNativeFileId + symbol mangling)
src/codegen/replacements.ts:168 ("$zig" in the macro list)
src/js/** — 24 $zig( call sites
src/js/private.d.ts — the $zig type declaration
build/debug/codegen/GeneratedJS2Native.h (generated; verify symbol names still resolve)

b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (also reproduced on 1.3.6, where the gap was larger)
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 (Apple M4, macOS 26.5.1)
What steps will reproduce the bug?
await-heavy code (an await on nearly every call) runs ~1.7× slower on Bun than on Node, and ~1.3× slower than Deno. Minimal repro, await-bench.mjs:
const fib = async n => n === 0 ? 0 : n === 1 ? 1 : await fib(n - 1) + await fib(n - 2);
await fib(20); // warmup
const t0 = performance.now();
const r = await fib(28);
console.log(`async fib(28): ${(performance.now() - t0).toFixed(0)} ms (=${r})`);
Median of 7 runs each:



runtime
median
min




Node v25.4.0
71 ms
49 ms


Deno 2.8.3
91 ms
84 ms


Bun 1.3.14
119 ms
115 ms



Two related observations:

Bun 1.3.6 measured ~136 ms on the same machine, so something between 1.3.7–1.3.14 already improved this — but the gap to Node is still ~1.7×.
The penalty compounds when an async function's result passes through another async function that just returns it (an extra promise layer). Wrapping the callee in async function (a) { return f(a); } vs a plain function (a) { return f(a); }: Node 95→60 ms, Bun 333→137 ms (1.3.6) — i.e. the wrapper costs 2.4× on Bun vs 1.6× on Node.

What is the expected behavior?
Comparable per-await cost to V8-based runtimes. V8 optimized await on already-resolved/non-promise values down to a single microtask tick years ago; this benchmark suggests JSC-on-Bun pays substantially more per await/async-frame.
What do you see instead?
~1.7× slower than Node on await-per-call code.
Additional information
Real-world context: ShenScript (a compiler from the Shen language to JS) emits async-everywhere code so Shen programs can do transparent async I/O — every Shen-level call is an awaited async call. Its kernel certification suite (134 tests, millions of awaited calls) runs in ~19 s on Node v25.4.0 and ~18 s on Deno 2.8.3, but ~50 s on Bun 1.3.6, tracking the micro-benchmark gap. Bun's startup and AOT/sync-path performance are otherwise excellent on the same codebase — this is specifically the awaited-async-call path.

t: Bun Shell: prefix assignment of an existing env var duplicates the environ entry (child sees the old value)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (also present in canary source)
What platform is your computer?
Linux x64 (WSL2), not platform-specific
What steps can reproduce the bug?
import { $ } from "bun";
console.log(await $`HOME=/tmp/zz env`.text());
What is the expected behavior?
One HOME= line, with the assigned value — a VAR=value cmd prefix
assignment should replace the inherited entry in the child environment.
What do you see instead?
Two HOME= lines: the inherited value first, then the assigned one:
HOME=/home/me
...
HOME=/tmp/zz

Since glibc's getenv returns the first match, the child program
effectively sees the old value — the prefix assignment is worse than
ignored, it's silently inverted.
The same happens when the variable was created earlier in the same script:
export FOO=first; FOO=second env shows both FOO=first and FOO=second.
export of an existing variable is fine (correctly replaces), and a fresh
variable (FOO=x FOO=y env) is fine — the duplication is specific to the
prefix-assignment path.
Cause
In SpawnArgs::fill_env (src/runtime/shell/subproc.rs, same logic in the
Zig original), the child environ is built by appending key=value lines
from export_env and then from cmd_local_env, with no dedup between the
two calls — a variable present in both maps lands in env_array twice.

t: Bun does not upgrade and hangs when using `node:http`
bun build --format=esm emits strict-invalid output for CommonJS files referencing unbound reserved words
b:
What
A CommonJS-classified file that references an unbound strict-mode reserved word bundles without error, but the emitted ESM output cannot be loaded:
$ cat u.mjs
exports.x = 1;
console.log(package);
$ bun build u.mjs --format=esm --outfile=out.mjs
$ bun out.mjs
2 | console.log(package);
                ^
error: "package" is a reserved word and cannot be used in strict mode
The renamer remaps bound reserved-word symbols (var package becomes _package via strict_mode_reserved_word_remap), but an unbound reference is not a scope member, so it survives verbatim into the always-strict ESM output.
Reproduces on 1.3.14 and current main, so it is not a regression. #32177 keeps this behavior unchanged: its deferred strict-mode queue records the feature in e_identifier before find_symbol resolves the ref, so boundness is not known at that point and the ESM-output-format check skips ReservedWord entirely to avoid failing the (valid) bound case.
Possible fix
Record boundness when e_identifier marks StrictModeFeature::ReservedWord (after find_symbol, the symbol kind distinguishes unbound refs), and let the ESM-output-format check in flush_deferred_forced_esm_strict_features fail the build only for unbound references, which are the ones that really survive into the output.
Surfaced by review of #32177.

t: `MySQL` error on querying `year` + `json` types, `year` returns as `Buffer`
Transpiler reserved-word check misses declarations in implicitly strict files (engine reports it at runtime instead)
b:
What
The parser's reserved-word check for declarations runs in declare_symbol during the parse pass (src/js_parser/p.rs), before implicit strict mode is applied in prepare_for_visit_pass (import/export/top-level-await keywords, class bodies, and the forced-ESM module type from #32177). So declarations like
export {};
let package = 1;
produce no transpiler diagnostic. The visit-pass check (visit_expr.rs, EIdentifier) only covers references, not binding positions.
The user-visible outcome is still a SyntaxError because the emitted module is evaluated in module goal by JSC:
$ cat b.mjs
let package = 1;
$ bun b.mjs
SyntaxError: Cannot use the reserved word 'package' as a lexical variable name in strict mode.
so this is a diagnostics-source gap (engine error at runtime instead of a transpiler error with a note naming the strict-mode reason), not a correctness bug. It applies to every implicit strict kind, not just the forced-ESM one, and has existed since before the Rust port.
Possible fix
Either run a binding-position reserved-word check during the visit pass (where scope strictness is known, mirroring the EvalOrArguments handling in visit/mod.rs), or give declare_symbol a parse-time notion of pending implicit strictness. The deferral queue added in #32177 (deferred_forced_esm_strict_features) can be reused so CommonJS-classified forced-ESM files keep their sloppy interop.
Surfaced by review of #32177.

t: bun test exits after failures are not LSan-clean (bail and failing runs abort under detect_leaks=1)
b:
Follow-up from #32180 (which makes green bun test exits LSan-clean). Runs that end in failure still abort under ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1 when BUN_DESTRUCT_VM_ON_EXIT is not set, turning an intended exit 1 into exit 134. Three distinct mechanisms, found while evaluating a review suggestion on #32180:


Ordinary failing test with --bail: CommandLineReporter::handle_test_completed (src/runtime/cli/test_command.rs, the bail branch around line 1374) calls Global::exit(1) directly. No deinit_for_exit(), no RUNNER clear, no final collection, and the active file is mid-execution at that point, so the straightforward fix (running the exec tail's teardown there) is not obviously safe: the run loop still holds the BunTestCell strong and BunTest::run frames may be live.


Module-evaluation-failure bail in TestCommand::run (the Status::Rejected branch around line 3179): runs deinit_for_exit() and clears RUNNER but exits without the final collection added in #32180, so wrapper boxes created before the bail (Expect, RefData, RcInner<BunTestCell>) stay malloc-live.


Any failing run, including through the exec tail: printing the failure caches a ParsedSourceMap Arc in vm.saved_source_map_table (SavedSourceMap::get_with_content, src/jsc/SavedSourceMap.rs:365, reached via remap_zig_exception). LSan cannot scan the table's backing memory, so the Arc is reported even though it is live VM state:


Direct leak of 168 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
    <alloc::sync::Arc<bun_sourcemap::parsed_source_map::ParsedSourceMap>>::new
    <bun_jsc::saved_source_map::SavedSourceMap>::get_with_content  src/jsc/SavedSourceMap.rs:365
    <bun_jsc::virtual_machine::VirtualMachine>::remap_zig_exception  src/jsc/VirtualMachine.rs:5324

Repro (debug ASAN build):
mkdir /tmp/fail-leak && cd /tmp/fail-leak
printf 'import { expect } from "bun:test";\nexpect(1 + 1).toBe(3);\n' > a.test.js
ASAN_OPTIONS="allow_user_segv_handler=1:disable_coredump=0:detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1" \
LSAN_OPTIONS="malloc_context_size=30:print_suppressions=0:suppressions=$BUN_REPO/test/leaksan.supp" \
bun-debug test .          # exit 134 (mechanism 3)
bun-debug test --bail .   # exit 134 (mechanisms 2 and 3)
No CI exposure today: every test that spawns bun test --bail is listed in test/no-validate-leaksan.txt (bun-test.test.ts, parallel.test.ts, regression/issue/12250.test.ts), and the CI leak lane sets BUN_DESTRUCT_VM_ON_EXIT=1, whose destroy() path frees the source-map table, so mechanism 3

What happens
On the 13 x64-asan CI lane, test/js/bun/http/serve-body-leak.test.ts intermittently fails its absolute end-memory cap:
expect(report.end_memory).toBeLessThanOrEqual(512 * 1024 * 1024);
Expected: <= 536870912
Received: 542494720

Example: build 62074 ("should not leak memory when buffering a JSON body"). The growth metric the test exists for (report.leak, allowed up to 64 MB) was 1 MB in the failing run, i.e. memory was flat; only the absolute RSS cap tripped.
Cause
Under ASAN, redzones inflate the fixture's RSS so the JSON-buffering test's steady-state end memory sits at roughly 490-515 MB, which straddles the hard 512 MB cap with about 0-5% headroom. The cap fails whichever build's noise lands a few MB higher on a given run.
Verified on unmodified main 885c44fea1 (release-asan build, CI's ASAN/LSAN env, running only the JSON-buffering test):

main, 14 runs: end_memory 488-513 MB, 1 run failed the 512 MB cap (end 513 MB, leak metric 23 MB, still under the 64 MB allowance)
a PR branch with unrelated changes, 14 interleaved runs: end_memory 492-515 MB, 2 runs failed

The distributions are indistinguishable; both cross the cap at a few-percent rate per run on the same machine. Per the repo guidance, RSS thresholds need ~2x headroom; this one has effectively none on the ASAN lane.
Possible fixes
Scale the absolute end_memory cap for ASAN builds (e.g. detect via Bun.version build flavor or an env flag and use 768 MB-1 GB), or drop the absolute cap on the ASAN lane and rely on the growth metric (leak <= 64 MB) plus the peak <= start * 2.5 ratio, which are the assertions that actually detect leaking.

b:
What happens
On the 13 x64-asan CI lane, test/regression/issue/30205.test.ts intermittently fails with the inner bun test --isolate subprocess exiting 134 after a fully green run (stderr contains 8 pass, 0 fail, Ran 8 tests across 8 files., then the process aborts). Examples: build 62070 (hard fail), build 62056 and build 61811 (passed on retry).
Cause
The CI test runner sets ASAN_OPTIONS=...detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1 and LSAN_OPTIONS=...suppressions=test/leaksan.supp (scripts/runner.node.mjs), and these propagate into subprocesses spawned with bunEnv. At exit of a bun test --isolate run, the last file's test-runner objects are still malloc-live: the Expect wrapper box, its RefData (freed only by Expect::finalize, which requires the wrapper to be GC-finalized), and the file's BunTestCell Rc. LSan reports them as leaks (~600 bytes, 11 allocations in the 30205 fixture), and abort_on_error=1 turns the report into SIGABRT, so a test asserting exitCode === 0 sees 134.
Whether the last file's wrappers get collected before exit is GC-timing dependent, which is why the lane only fails sometimes.

t: Parser does not apply implicit strict mode to files forced to ESM by .mjs or package.json "type": "module"
b:
What
The parser applies implicit strict mode only when a file contains import/export syntax or top-level await (src/js_parser/p.rs, the recursive_set_strict_mode block in prepare_for_visit_pass). Files that are ES modules only because of their extension (.mjs/.mts) or package.json "type": "module" are parsed as sloppy mode. Per ECMA-262, module code is always strict, so Node rejects these:
$ cat with.mjs
with ({x: 1}) { console.log(x); }
$ node with.mjs
SyntaxError: Strict mode code may not include a with statement
$ bun with.mjs
1
Legacy octal literals behave the same way (exports.v = 010 in a .mjs file prints 8 in bun, SyntaxError in node). Strict mode also alters block-level function declaration hoisting, so scoping can differ from Node in these files too.
Why this is not a one-liner

Bun deliberately executes .mjs/"type": "module" files that use CommonJS features (exports.foo = ...) as CommonJS via interop. Forcing implicit strict mode at parse time would turn currently-working bun-specific files into hard parse errors even when they end up executing as CJS.
It needs a new StrictModeKind variant with its own "implicitly in strict mode because ..." message (the existing variants name the import/export/await keyword).
Hoisting changes are user-observable, so this needs its own test matrix and likely a maintainer decision on the interop question.

Surfaced during review of #32173, which only fixes the value of top-level this and does not change strict-mode classification.

t: pino transport (thread-stream worker) hangs ~10s on SIGINT/exit under Bun — `_flushSync took too long (10s)`; works on Node
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14 (macOS arm64) — also reproduced on Bun 1.3.x (Linux x64, production under pm2)
What platform is your computer?
Darwin arm64 (macOS) / Linux x64
What steps can reproduce the bug?
Any pino logger configured with a transport (e.g. pino-pretty) spawns a worker thread via thread-stream. On process termination, thread-stream.flushSync() blocks on Atomics.wait waiting for the worker to drain the shared buffer. Under Bun the worker never advances, so it hangs until the internal 10s timeout and throws.
repro.mjs:
import pino from 'pino'
const logger = pino({ transport: { target: 'pino-pretty' } })
logger.info('alive; send SIGINT')
setInterval(() => {}, 1000) // keep process alive
bun add pino pino-pretty
bun repro.mjs      # then press Ctrl+C (SIGINT)

What is the expected behavior?
The process exits promptly on SIGINT, flushing the transport — exactly as Node.js does:
node repro.mjs  →  Ctrl+C  →  exits in ~0.0s

What do you see instead?
The process hangs ~10–17s after SIGINT before dying. When an uncaughtException handler wraps the process (e.g. pm2), it surfaces as a crash:
error: _flushSync took too long (10s)
    at flushSync (thread-stream)
    at onExit2 (on-exit-leak-free)




Runtime
SIGINT → exit




Bun 1.3.14
~17s (hang)


Node v24.14.0
~0.0s



Same code, same node_modules.
Additional information

Root cause appears to be worker_threads + SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics.wait not coordinating on the exit/flush path: the main thread blocks in Atomics.wait, the worker never drains/notifies, so it times out after 10s.
Affects any pino transport (pino-pretty, pino/file, log rotation), not just pretty-printing.
Real-world impact: under pm2, every pm2 reload (which sends SIGINT) triggers this; combined with pm2's uncaughtException instrumentation it kills the process.
Workaround: avoid pino transports on Bun — log plain JSON to stdout and pipe to pino-pretty as a separate process (bun app.js | pino-pretty).

t: napi: NapiFinalizerTask boxes leak at exit when the final GC sweeps deferred finalizers (LSAN failure in 30205 isolate test on asan CI)
b:
On the debian x64-asan CI lane, test/regression/issue/30205.test.ts (--isolate: deferred napi finalizers from the previous global don't write to its dead cell) intermittently fails with exit 134 after all 8 inner tests pass. With the inner stderr now surfaced (#31959, commit e20464e), the actual failure is a LeakSanitizer report at process exit:
==5438==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
Direct leak of 31904 byte(s) in 997 object(s) allocated from:
    ...
    #8 new<bun_runtime::napi::napi_body::NapiFinalizerTask>
    #9 init      src/runtime/napi/napi_body.rs:4243
    #10 enqueue  src/runtime/napi/napi_body.rs:2369
    #11 napi_internal_enqueue_finalizer src/runtime/napi/napi_body.rs:2396
    #12 Zig::NapiRef::callFinalizer()   src/jsc/bindings/napi.h:742
    #13 Napi::NapiRefSelfDeletingWeakHandleOwner::finalize src/jsc/bindings/napi.cpp:273
    #14-23 JSC::WeakBlock::sweep / MarkedSpace::sweepBlocks / Heap::collectNow
    #24 Zig__GlobalObject__destructOnExit src/jsc/bindings/ZigGlobalObject.cpp:3966
    #25 VirtualMachine::global_exit       src/jsc/VirtualMachine.rs:1581

Mechanism: the final collectNow() in Zig__GlobalObject__destructOnExit sweeps the last test file's ~1000 napi-wrapped objects. Their deferred finalizers go through NapiFinalizerTask::schedule() (src/runtime/napi/napi_body.rs:4247). That function already has exit handling: when vm.is_shutting_down() && vm.has_run_cleanup_hooks() it drops the task, and when shutting down without hooks run it registers a cleanup hook. The leak means the tasks are landing in a sink that is never drained at that point in teardown, either the cleanup-hook list after its final walk or the immediate task queue of a loop that never ticks again, so 997 Box<NapiFinalizerTask> (plus their NapiEnvRefs) are still live when LSAN scans.
Repro: the exact scenario is the --isolate test in test/regression/issue/30205.test.ts (8 files x 1000 addon.wrap(...) with BUN_JSC_collectContinuously=1). It does not reproduce on a local debug ASAN build even with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 (the run shows only the usual suppressed exit allocations), so the branch taken in schedule() appears to depend on teardown timing that differs on the release-asan CI build. Observed on builds 61984 and 61990 (https://buildkite.com/bun/bun/builds/61990), both times on the shard running this file.
This is unrelated to the SSL/proxy change in #31959 (the fixtures do no networking); it will intermittently fail any PR whose asan shard pick

t: Error.captureStackTrace(err, fn) removes too many frames — zod v4 .parse() errors end up with an empty stack
sql.listen() subscription does not keep the process alive while waiting for notifications
b:
What is the problem?
A process whose only pending work is an active sql.listen() subscription exits instead of staying alive to receive notifications:
import { SQL } from "bun";
const sql = new SQL("postgres://localhost/db");
await sql.listen("events", payload => console.log(payload));
// process exits here; it should stay alive waiting for NOTIFY
postgres.js keeps the process alive in this situation (the dedicated listen connection holds the event loop), so long-running listeners "just work" without an artificial keepalive.
What I found
The adapter calls conn.ref() on the dedicated listen connection (src/js/internal/sql/postgres.ts, #createListenConnection), and the native side confirms poll_ref is in the Active state after the LISTEN query completes. Tracing the uws loop counters (debug scope Loop in src/uws_sys/Loop.rs) with a subscribed-only child process shows:
[loop] ref 1 + 1 = 2 | 0 + 1 = 1        <- connect path
[postgres] SET_STATUS Connected, poll_ref.unref()
[loop] unref 2 - 1 = 1 | 1 - 1 = 0
[postgres] update_ref: count=1, ref
[loop] ref 1 + 1 = 2 | 0 + 1 = 1
[postgres] LISTEN completes (update_ref no-ops, already Active)
SUBSCRIBED                               <- top-level await done
[loop] unref 2 - 1 = 1 | 1 - 1 = 0      <- unlogged caller, active hits 0, process exits

The final unref does not come from the Postgres connection (its poll_ref is still Active) or from the JS adapter; some other component releases an active count it did not pair with the connection's ref, so the loop's active reaches 0 while the connection believes it is holding the process alive. The same accounting predates the LISTEN/NOTIFY feature (the conn.ref()/update_ref interplay is inherited from the pooled-connection lifecycle), but LISTEN is the first consumer that needs an idle-yet-referenced connection.
Notes
Found while working on #32089 (which added LISTEN/NOTIFY). Out of scope there: the fix is in the native event-loop keepalive accounting shared by all SQL connections, not in the LISTEN feature. #32089 closes the dedicated connection when the last subscription is removed, so once this is fixed the lifecycle will be: subscribed = process alive, last unlisten = connection closed and process free.

t: Bun.Image: Blob read dispatch failure leaks the read chain and pins the wrapper
b:
In src/runtime/image/Image.rs, BlobReadChain::start() increments pending_tasks, upgrades this_ref to Strong, and leaks the chain Box into a raw pointer before calling blob.read_bytes_to_handler(). If that call returns Err (reachable through the S3 arm: download()/download_slice() can fail at dispatch time), nothing is unwound:

pending_tasks stays incremented, so this_ref stays Strong forever and the Image wrapper can never be collected
the BlobReadChain allocation (and its JSPromiseStrong and any WriteDest Strong) leaks

A fix needs to audit ownership of the S3 Task pointer inside Blob.rs read_bytes_to_handler for the same Err: it is heap::into_raw'd before the fallible dispatch, so it may need the same unwind, and the Image-side cleanup must not double-free if the S3 layer already invoked the callback with a failure.
Pre-existing behavior, surfaced by review on #32123 (which only touches the success path of this function).

t: Bun.Image: remaining gaps for replacing Sharp in a production photo pipeline (clone(), stats()/dominant color, content-aware crop, encode options, metadata, timeout)
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
We run a production photo pipeline on Bun: every upload fans out into 7 delivery variants (smart-cropped cards, squares, true-aspect srcset rungs, a 1200×630 OG/social JPEG, a tiny LQIP), plus a perceptual hash and a dominant color for placeholder backgrounds. Today this uses Sharp for decode/resize/crop/ICC.
We'd love to replace that stack with Bun.Image, and most of the building blocks already exist: autoOrient by default, maxPixels, fit: "inside" + withoutEnlargement, resize filter selection, ICC profile preservation (#30201 / #30211), S3 integration, placeholder().
Below are the remaining gaps, each with its concrete production use case. Related items that are already tracked are linked rather than re-requested here: fit: "cover" + position anchors (#31502), AVIF encode on Linux (#30199 — a hard prerequisite for any Linux server pipeline), raw pixel access (#30622), fit: "contain" / background / animated (#30731), composite (#30628), trim() (#30615).
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
1. clone() — decode once, fan out many pipelines
const base = new Bun.Image(upload, { maxPixels: 100_000_000 });
const [card, square, max1920, social] = await Promise.all([
  base.clone().resize(1280, 1024, { fit: "cover" }).avif({ quality: 60 }).bytes(),
  base.clone().resize(640, 640, { fit: "cover" }).avif({ quality: 60 }).bytes(),
  base.clone().resize(1920, 1920, { fit: "inside", withoutEnlargement: true }).avif({ quality: 60 }).bytes(),
  base.clone().resize(1200, 630, { fit: "cover" }).jpeg({ quality: 82 }).bytes(),
]);
With 7 variants per upload, re-decoding a 12MP source 7 times dominates the cost. Sharp's clone() shares the decoded input across pipelines; Bun.Image's lazy pipeline model looks well suited to the same optimization (share the decode, fork the transform chains).
2. stats() — dominant color (and basic image statistics)
const { dominant } = await img.stats(); // { r, g, b }
We store a dominant color per photo and paint it behind the image before the LQIP/full image loads. Sharp computes this from a 4096-bin 3D histogram in stats(), which also exposes per-channel min/max/mean/stdev and entropy/sharpness — useful for blur/quality heuristics at upload time. Even a minimal { dominant } would remove a Sharp dependency for a very common social/media-app need.
3. Content-aware crop position + explicit region crop
#31502 requests fixed anchors (position: "top", etc.). The complementary ask

t: coverageSkipTestFiles does not exclude test files from coverage threshold
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14+0d9b296af
What platform is your computer?
Linux 6.12.90 x86_64 x86_64
What steps can reproduce the bug?

Set up bunfig.toml with threshold and skip test files:

[test]
coverageThreshold = { lines = 0.8, functions = 0.8, statements = 0.8 }
coverageSkipTestFiles = true


Have source files with good coverage (>80%) and test files with 0% coverage.


Run:


bun test --coverage

→ exits 1 even though all source files exceed the threshold
What is the expected behavior?
coverageSkipTestFiles = true should skip test files when computing coverage statistics (as documented), including the threshold check. Only source files should count against the threshold.
What do you see instead?
Test files are hidden from the display table but still counted in the threshold check. Since test files have 0% coverage (nothing tests the tests), the per-file threshold fails even when all source files easily meet it.
Additional information
Workaround: use coveragePathIgnorePatterns = ["tests/**"] instead, which properly excludes from both display and threshold. This was added in #21013.
Related: #17028 -- the per-file threshold behavior compounds this, since a single 0%-coverage test file fails the whole run.

t: bun test --coverage-reporter=lcov skips coverage threshold check
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14+0d9b296af
What platform is your computer?
Linux 6.12.90 x86_64 x86_64
What steps can reproduce the bug?

Set an unreachable coverage threshold in bunfig.toml:

[test]
coverageThreshold = { lines = 1.0, functions = 1.0, statements = 1.0 }
coveragePathIgnorePatterns = ["tests/**"]

Run with bare --coverage:

bun test --coverage

→ exits 1 (correct)

Run with --coverage-reporter=lcov:

bun test --coverage --coverage-reporter=lcov

→ exits 0 (wrong -- coverage is way below the 100% threshold)
What is the expected behavior?
--coverage-reporter should not affect whether the threshold is enforced. Exit code 1 when coverage is below threshold, regardless of reporter flags.
What do you see instead?
With --coverage-reporter=lcov, the threshold check is silently skipped. All tests pass, the coverage table prints, the lcov file is generated, exit code 0 -- but coverage was actually far below the configured threshold.
Additional information
This is easy to miss because the runner still prints the coverage table -- everything looks fine in CI logs. The workaround is to run two separate bun test invocations: one bare --coverage for the threshold check, then --coverage --coverage-reporter=lcov for the file.

t: Support `bin` field in `bun info` / `bun pm view` output
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
npm view <pkg> bin (and pnpm view <pkg> bin) displays the bin field from a package's metadata, showing the command-name-to-script mapping. For example:
% npm view run bin
{ runjs: 'cli.js' }

This is useful for quickly discovering what executables a package provides and what they're named. Bun's bun info <pkg> <field> / bun pm view <pkg> <field> supports querying many package metadata fields (version, dependencies, repository.url, etc.), but the bin field either doesn't return the expected output or isn't handled equivalently to npm/pnpm.
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
Ensure bun info <pkg> bin and bun pm view <pkg> bin return the same structured output as npm view <pkg> bin — a JSON object mapping command names to their entry point scripts. This should work for:

Packages with a single bin string (should still return the object form)
Packages with a bin object mapping multiple commands
Scoped packages (@scope/pkg)
Versioned queries (pkg@1.2.3)

What alternatives have you considered?

Using bun info <pkg> --json and parsing the full JSON output to extract the bin field manually — works but defeats the purpose of the field-specific query syntax.
Using npm view as a fallback — works but requires npm to be installed, which isn't guaranteed in Bun-first environments.

t: Bun.SQL: sql.close() hangs after closing a reserved connection with reserved.close()
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0 and main (f8723b1)
What is the problem?
Closing a reserved connection directly with reserved.close() and then closing the pool hangs forever:
const sql = new Bun.SQL(url, { max: 2 });
const reserved = await sql.reserve();
await reserved`select 1`;
await reserved.close();   // resolves
await sql.close();        // never resolves
Output stops after the reserved close; the process has to be killed. Using reserved.release() instead of reserved.close() works, and sql.close() completes normally.
reserved_sql.close() calls pooledConnection.close() directly without going through the pool's release path, so the pool still counts the connection as checked out and close() waits for it indefinitely.
Reproduced against the docker-compose postgres service. Found while working on #32096 (the close timeout bound); this hang is independent of that bug and happens with no timeout option at all.

t: Bun.SQL: close() timeout upper bound is validated in seconds but armed in milliseconds
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0 and main (f8723b1)
What is the problem?
The close({ timeout }) validation in both pool adapters checks the upper bound against the seconds value, but the timer is armed in milliseconds:
if (timeout > 2 ** 31 || timeout < 0 || timeout !== timeout) {
  throw $ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE(...);
}
...
const timer = setTimeout(..., timeout * 1000);
setTimeout clamps delays above 2 ** 31 - 1 ms to 1 ms:
$ bun -e "const t=Date.now(); setTimeout(() => { console.log('fired after', Date.now()-t, 'ms'); }, 2**31 * 1000)"
TimeoutOverflowWarning: 2147483648000 does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer.
Timeout duration was set to 1.
fired after 3 ms
So any timeout in (2147483.647, 2 ** 31] seconds passes validation and then force-closes after about 1 ms, cancelling in-flight queries, instead of waiting the requested time.
Affected code

src/js/internal/sql/postgres.ts, PostgresAdapter.close()
src/js/internal/sql/mysql.ts, MySQLAdapter.close()
src/js/bun/sql.ts, reserved_sql.close() and transaction_sql.close() (same bound, same timeout * 1000)

The bound should be 2 ** 31 / 1000 (or the validation should run on the millisecond product).
Split out from the investigation of #32091.

t: node-net.test.ts: un-awaited expectMaxObjectTypeCount in named-pipe test fails unrelated subsequent tests on Windows
b:
test/js/node/net/node-net.test.ts line 856, inside the Windows-only test should work with named pipes:
expectMaxObjectTypeCount(expect, "TCPSocket", before);
expectMaxObjectTypeCount is async (it polls heapStats() with Bun.sleep between GC passes), but this call site does not await it. Two consequences:

The assertion is vacuous for the named-pipe test itself: the test completes before the poll finishes, so a leak can never fail it.
The floating promise keeps polling across test boundaries, and when its final expect(...).toBeLessThanOrEqual(...) fails, the failure is attributed to whichever test happens to be running at that moment. This was observed in build https://buildkite.com/bun/bun/builds/61865 on the Windows lanes: tests added after the named-pipe test failed with expectMaxObjectTypeCount ... Expected: <= 0, Received: 5 even though they never call that helper and create no TCPSocket objects.

Note that just adding await may make the named-pipe test itself fail on Windows: in the build above, the TCPSocket count was still 5 more than before after well over a second of polling, so either the count genuinely does not settle (possible handle leak across ~700 named-pipe connections, worth investigating on its own) or the poll window is too short for Windows CI.
This is the only un-awaited expectMaxObjectTypeCount call site in the repo.

Linux (observed on x64 Cloud Run and arm64 Docker). The bug is platform-independent arithmetic.
What's the bug?
writeOrEndBuffered in src/bun.js/api/bun/socket.zig mis-accounts which bytes of the new chunk remain unsent after a partial vectored write when there is already natively-buffered data. Depending on where the kernel cuts the write, it either re-buffers bytes that were already written (→ duplicated bytes on the wire) or skips bytes that were never written (→ silent data loss).
Permalinks:

v1.2.14: https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/bun-v1.2.14/src/bun.js/api/bun/socket.zig#L2314-L2315
v1.3.6: https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/blob/bun-v1.3.6/src/bun.js/api/bun/socket.zig#L989-L990

// fast-ish path: use writev() to avoid cloning to another buffer.
const rc = this.socket.socket.connected.write2(ssl, this.buffered_data_for_node_net.slice(), buffer.slice());
const written: usize = @intCast(@max(rc, 0));
const leftover = total_to_write -| written;
if (leftover == 0) { ... break :brk rc; }

const remaining_in_buffered_data = this.buffered_data_for_node_net.slice()[@min(written, this.buffered_data_for_node_net.len)..];
const remaining_in_input_data = buffer.slice()[@min(this.buffered_data_for_node_net.len -| written, buffer.slice().len)..];
write2 writes the old buffered data B first, then the new chunk I. The number of bytes of I consumed by the kernel is written -| B.len. The code computes B.len -| written — the saturating subtraction is reversed.
remaining_in_buffered_data is correct; remaining_in_input_data is not.
Case analysis
Let b = B.len, n = I.len, w = written, with 0 < w < b + n (the full-write case returns early and is fine):
| case | bytes of I actually consumed | what the code keeps: I[min(b -| w, n)..] | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| w > b | w - b | I[0..] (the whole chunk) | first w - b bytes of I are buffered again → sent twice |
| w == b | 0 | I[0..] | correct |
| w < b | 0 | I[min(b - w, n)..] | first min(b - w, n) bytes of I are never sent and never buffered → lost (the entire chunk is lost when b - w >= n) |
Expected fix
const remaining_in_input_data = buffer.slice()[@min(written -| this.buffered_data_for_node_net.len, buffer.slice().len)..];
This is unit-testable in isolation by driving the function with a mocked write2 returning partial counts on either side of b.
Reachabi

t: globalStore cache paths with @/+ characters break Vite 7.3+ ModuleRunner on Windows
b:
Bug Description
When globalStore = true is set in bunfig.toml, bun creates cache directories with @ and + characters in their names (e.g., crossws@0.4.6+cdd8242261126fe3...).
Vite 7.3's ModuleRunner converts these file paths to file:// URLs without percent-encoding the + character, which is interpreted as a space in URL encoding. This causes ERR_LOAD_URL — Vite can't find the module.
Steps to Reproduce

Windows 10/11
bunfig.toml with [install] globalStore = true
Any Vite 7.3+ project (Nuxt, TanStack Start, Nitro, etc.)
bun install && bun run dev
ERR_LOAD_URL on module load

Environment

Bun: 1.3.14
OS: Windows 10 / 11
Vite: 7.3+

Possible Bun-side fixes

Percent-encode + and @ in global cache directory names (e.g., crossws%400.4.6%2Bcdd824...)
Use only filesystem-safe characters in cache paths (replace @ → -at-, + → -plus-)
Document the incompatibility with Vite 7.3+ ModuleRunner when globalStore is enabled on Windows

Workaround for users
Delete ~/.bunfig.toml (or remove globalStore = true) and reinstall with bun's default linker.
Vite issue
Cross-filed at vitejs/vite#22662 (Vite should also percent-encode paths when constructing file:// URLs)

t: Worker lifetime: carry a generation token with cross-thread VM handles (follow-up to #32071)
b:
Follow-up to #32071, which added a process-global registry of live VM/event-loop addresses so cross-thread producers (HTTP client thread, work pool, watcher threads, napi addon threads) stop enqueueing into a terminated worker's freed VirtualMachine.
The registry keys liveness by address only. That leaves a known residual: if a new VM is allocated at a dead VM's address, a stale producer that captured the old pointer passes the check and its completion is delivered to the new VM instead of being dropped. This mis-delivery predates the registry (the stale push landed at the same reused address before, plus all the freed-memory interleavings that are now closed), so #32071 strictly narrows the exposure, but closing it fully needs a non-reused identity.
A registry-side generation counter is not sufficient on its own: producers only bring an address to the lookup, so the token has to be captured at schedule time and carried by the producer. Proposed shape:

VmHandle { addr: usize, gen: u64 } (Copy), handed out by live_vm_registry::register_vm and VirtualMachine::concurrent_handle().
Checked entry points (VirtualMachine::try_enqueue_task_concurrent, EventLoop::try_enqueue_task_concurrent, with_live_vm, is_shutting_down_or_freed, try_ref/unref_concurrently) accept the handle and verify (addr, gen) under the registry lock.
Every producer struct that today stores *mut VirtualMachine / BackRef<EventLoop> for completion delivery (FetchTasklet, S3 tasks, WorkTask, ConcurrentPromiseTask, AnyTaskJob, node:fs async tasks, zlib native streams, napi async_work/TSFN/finalizer, watchers, PasswordObject, bundler completion, EventLoopHandle) switches to the handle.

Related: the same follow-up is the natural place to close TSFN acceptance on dead worker VMs (today a rejected dispatch leaves the queue accepting undeliverable work; see the discussion on #32071) together with the napi env teardown work tracked in #15964 item 4 and #30286.

t: Uppercase 'data:' URL schemes are rejected by the module resolver (Node accepts them)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0 (latest main)
What is the problem?
URL schemes are case-insensitive (RFC 3986; the WHATWG URL parser lowercases them), and Node accepts uppercase data: module specifiers. Bun's module resolver rejects them before any data URL handling runs:
const m = await import('DATA:text/javascript,export const x=1');
console.log(Object.keys(m));
$ node main.mjs
[ 'x' ]

$ bun main.mjs
error: Cannot find module 'DATA:text/javascript,export const x=1' from '/tmp/main.mjs'
Data:, dAtA:, etc. behave the same.
Notes
Every data: check in the pipeline is lowercase-only, so fixing this needs scheme normalization at the resolver rather than loosening one call site:

module resolution (produces the "Cannot find module" above)
DataURL::parse in src/resolver/data_url.rs (starts_with(b"data:"))
the runtime loader gate in src/runtime/jsc_hooks.rs and the transpiler contents path in src/bundler/transpiler.rs (both has_prefix_comptime(path.text, b"data:"))

Split out of a review thread on #32059, which only covers lowercase data: loader selection.

t: data: URL JS module collapses ESM → CJS (named exports lost) when an exported binding gets a property assignment
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.11 (Linux x64)
What is the problem?
import() of a non-base64 data:text/javascript URL returns
{ __esModule, default } instead of the module's named exports when the module
assigns a property to an exported binding (e.g. f.m = 1). The module is
silently treated as CommonJS and all named exports vanish.
A base64-encoded data: URL with the same source works correctly, and the
same source in a real .mjs/.js file also works correctly. Node and
browsers handle every form correctly.
Minimal reproduction
const code = 'export function f(){}\nf.m = 1\nexport const x = 1\n'

// percent-encoded data: URL
const percent = await import('data:text/javascript,' + encodeURIComponent(code))
console.log(Object.keys(percent)) // ["__esModule","default"]  ← bug

// base64 data: URL (same source)
const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(code)
let bin = ''; for (const b of bytes) bin += String.fromCharCode(b)
const base64 = await import('data:text/javascript;base64,' + btoa(bin))
console.log(Object.keys(base64)) // ["f","x"]  ← correct
What should have happened?
Both imports should yield the named exports ["f", "x"]. The module is
unambiguously ESM (it has export statements).
Additional findings

Trigger is specifically a member assignment on an exported binding
(export function f(){}; f.m = 1). Without that assignment, percent-encoded
modules round-trip fine.
data:-specific: the identical source imported from a .mjs file yields
["f","x"]. Only the data: URL path collapses — so this is not general
CJS detection.
MIME type is irrelevant: text/javascript, application/javascript,
text/ecmascript, application/ecmascript, ;charset=utf-8, and even no MIME
(data:,…) all collapse under percent-encoding. Only the encoding matters:
percent → CJS collapse, base64 → correct ESM.

Impact
tjs-lang emits fn.__tjs = { … } metadata on every typed function, so any
tjs-compiled module loaded via a percent-encoded data: URL (the natural way to
run transpiled code in the browser/playground without writing a file) hits this.

t: fs utimes-family errors report syscall "utimensat" instead of Node's "utime"/"lutime"
S3Client ignores NO_PROXY when HTTP_PROXY is set
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0 (reproduces on current main)
What steps can reproduce the bug?
With HTTP_PROXY pointing at a proxy and NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1:
const server = Bun.serve({ port: 0, fetch: () => new Response("ok") });

// fetch honors NO_PROXY: connects directly, prints "ok"
console.log(await (await fetch(server.url)).text());

// S3Client does not: the request is sent to HTTP_PROXY instead of the local endpoint
await Bun.S3Client.file("key", {
  accessKeyId: "test",
  secretAccessKey: "test",
  region: "eu-west-3",
  bucket: "my_bucket",
  endpoint: server.url.href,
}).write("content");
What is the expected behavior?
S3 requests to hosts listed in NO_PROXY / no_proxy bypass the proxy, the same way fetch does.
What do you see instead?
The S3 request is tunneled through HTTP_PROXY and fails (or hits the wrong server). The mock server is never reached.
Additional information
EnvLoader::get_http_proxy(is_http, hostname, host) only applies the NO_PROXY filter when hostname is Some. The fetch path passes the request URL (get_http_proxy_for(&url) in src/runtime/webcore/fetch/FetchTasklet.rs), but every S3 call site passes None, None, so the filter is skipped:

src/runtime/webcore/S3File.rs (3 sites)
src/runtime/webcore/Blob.rs
src/runtime/webcore/blob/Store.rs (2 sites)
src/runtime/webcore/ReadableStream.rs

The effective request host (endpoint option, virtual hosted style, bucket, region) is resolved later during signing, so the fix probably belongs where the signed URL is known rather than at those call sites.
This also makes any test suite that points S3Client at a local mock server fail in proxied environments, e.g. test/js/bun/s3/s3-requester-pays.test.ts.

t: Response API accepts invalid Response objects (non-WHATWG compliant)
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.14+0d9b296af
What platform is your computer?
Darwin 24.6.0 arm64 arm
What steps can reproduce the bug?
Run this with Bun:
for (const status of [204, 205, 304, 200]) {
  try {
    const res = new Response("body", { status })
    console.log(
      status,
      "ok",
      res.status,
      res.body === null ? "null-body" : "has-body",
    )
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(status, "throws", `${error.name}: ${error.message}`)
  }
}
For comparison, run the same snippet with Node.js:
bun repro.js
node repro.js

I tested the comparison against Node.js v25.9.0.
What is the expected behavior?
The Response constructor should throw a TypeError when a non-null body is provided with a null-body status.
The Fetch Standard defines 204, 205, and 304 as null-body statuses, and the initialize a response algorithm says:
If body is non-null, then: If response’s status is a null body status, then throw a TypeError.
Relevant spec links:
Null-body status definition: https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#null-body-status
Response initialization: https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#initialize-a-response
Expected output, matching Node.js/undici behavior:
204 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 204
205 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 205
304 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 304
200 ok 200 has-body

What do you see instead?
Bun accepts the invalid Response objects and preserves the body:
204 ok 204 has-body
205 ok 205 has-body
304 ok 304 has-body
200 ok 200 has-body

Node.js rejects the same invalid constructor calls:
204 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 204
205 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 205
304 throws TypeError: Response constructor: Invalid response status code 304
200 ok 200 has-body

Additional information
This can hide bugs in code that builds proxy responses or framework responses under Bun during tests, then crashes in production on Node.js/undici. The minimal issue is independent of any particular framework or server: new Response("body", { status: 204 }) should not construct a response with a body.
There is a related open issue, #20676, about Bun.serve emitting Content-Length for 204 responses. This issue seems adjacent but distinct: the Response constructor itself accepts a non-null body for null-body statuses, which the Fetch Standard says should throw.

t: Unterminated \u{ escape in string literals is accepted instead of raising a syntax error
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.4.0-canary.1+73ab3ddc7
What platform is your computer?
Linux x64
What steps can reproduce the bug?
An unterminated \u{ escape in a string literal is accepted and silently decoded instead of raising a syntax error:
$ bun -e 'console.log("\u{41")'
A
Node rejects the same input:
$ node -e 'console.log("\u{41")'
SyntaxError: Invalid unicode escape
The TOML parser has the same quirk (it supports \u{...} as an extension):
Bun.TOML.parse('a = "\\u{41"'); // { a: "A" }, no error
What is the expected behavior?
A syntax error, matching V8 and JSC: the escape is malformed because the closing } is missing.
What do you see instead?
The partial escape decodes as if it were terminated.
Additional information
The variable-length branch of the escape-sequence decoder breaks out of its digit loop when the input ends and falls through to emitting the accumulated value. Historically both copies of the decoder did this (src/js_parser/lexer.rs and src/parsers/toml/lexer.rs), and the shared decode_escape_sequences in src/ast/lexer_log.rs preserves it. Strict JSON mode is unaffected because it rejects \u{ before reading any digits.
This can only trigger when the string body itself ends inside the braces, i.e. the closing quote immediately follows the partial escape ("\u{41"), since an unterminated string errors earlier.

t: bunx ignores globally installed packages when using scoped package names (e.g. `bunx @scope/pkg`)
b:
What is the problem this feature would solve?
When a package is already installed globally via bun add -g, running bunx <pkg> still downloads and caches a separate copy instead of reusing the global install. This wastes disk space and network bandwidth.
Example:
bun add -g typescript       # installs to ~/.bun/install/global/node_modules/
bunx tsc --version          # downloads a NEW copy to ~/.bun/install/cache/ or /tmp/bunx-*/
bunx checks local node_modules first, then falls straight to the npm registry / cache — it never looks at ~/.bun/install/global/. This means every globally installed package you invoke via bunx gets duplicated on disk.
For users who install CLI tools globally (the common case for bunx usage), this results in redundant downloads and wasted storage.
What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?
bunx should check the global install directory ($BUN_INSTALL/global/node_modules/ or ~/.bun/install/global/node_modules/) before falling back to the npm cache / auto-install. If the requested package (at a compatible version) is already globally installed, bunx should use it directly.
Resolution order would become:

Local node_modules (current behavior)
Global install (new step)
npm cache / auto-install (current fallback)

This mirrors how npx in Node.js checks the global node_modules prefix before downloading.
What alternatives have you considered?

Manually running the global bin shim (e.g., tsc instead of bunx tsc) — works but defeats the purpose of bunx as a universal runner, and doesn't handle version pinning or scoped packages.
Symlinking global packages into a local node_modules — fragile and manual.
Accepting the duplication — wastes disk and bandwidth, especially painful on CI or constrained environments.

t: child_process cannot spawn native Windows executables (Rust-compiled) on Windows — hangs / ETIMEDOUT
MySQL: query writes can bypass queued-but-unwritten requests in the native request queue
b:
Follow-up from the postgres fix for #32004 (pool stall from wire order diverging from queue order).
The MySQL native queue has the same structural window, though it is harder to hit:

JSMySQLQuery::do_run (src/sql_jsc/mysql/JSMySQLQuery.rs) optimistically calls this.run(connection) before enqueue_request, and MySQLQuery::run's Status::Prepared arm writes Bind+Execute immediately when connection.can_pipeline() is true.
can_pipeline (src/sql_jsc/mysql/MySQLRequestQueue.rs) requires is_ready_for_query, which is false while a request is in flight, so the window is narrower than the postgres one. But several response handlers in src/sql_jsc/mysql/MySQLConnection.rs call queue.mark_as_ready_for_query() and then run a JS callback (resolve/reject) before self.advance(). User code in that callback can issue a new query whose run() sees is_ready_for_query == true and writes immediately, while an earlier queued-but-unwritten (Pending) request is still at the head of the queue.
Responses are matched to queue.current() in FIFO order, so a bypassed request would consume the new query's response packets, same as the postgres bug.

The postgres side was fixed by removing the immediate-write fast path from run() and letting advance() (which walks the queue in FIFO order and enforces the ordering barriers) do all writes. The MySQL equivalent would be to stop calling run() from do_run and pump the queue instead, but that needs its own verification and a deterministic repro (MySQL protocol mock including auth handshake) to prove fail-before.
Note: the pool-level fix from #32004 (reserved connections are no longer visible to flushConcurrentQueries) already applies to the MySQL adapter and removes the main real-world trigger (transactions sharing a connection with pooled queries).

t: SQL: connection pool stalls under concurrent begin() + parameterized queries (idle connections never handed to pending queries)
[Unsoundness] Reference-receiver to_js methods rely on prose heap-allocation contracts
b:
Follow-up to #31975 / #31984, which made the raw-pointer adoption surface (to_js(*mut T), to_js_unchecked, __create) unsafe fn.
One layer up, several safe methods take &self/&mut self and derive the m_ctx payload pointer from the reference, relying on a prose caller contract that the receiver is the class's construct-path heap allocation:

NewSourceCodegen::to_js(&mut self) (src/runtime/webcore/ReadableStream.rs); the finalizer ends in decrement_count -> heap::take
Request::to_js(&self) (src/runtime/webcore/Request.rs)
Response::to_js(&self) (src/runtime/webcore/Response.rs)
BlobExt::to_js(&self) (src/runtime/webcore/Blob.rs)
NewSocket::to_js(&self) (src/runtime/socket/socket_body.rs)

Safe crate-internal code can construct these types by value (several have all-pub fields, e.g. NewSource) and call the method on a stack value, after which GC finalization frees non-heap memory.
Fix direction: owning receivers (Box<Self> / a wrapper type produced by the heap constructor) or unsafe fn with the precondition in # Safety. Either way the change fans out widely (the .to_js(global) family alone has hundreds of call sites across Request/Response/Blob paths), so it needs its own PR rather than riding on #31984. Note a mi_is_in_heap_region runtime probe is not a sound guard: ASAN builds do not use mimalloc as the global allocator (see the existing comments on to_js_unchecked in Blob.rs / ArrayBufferSink.rs).

Source verification against origin/main a9886150983872820ddf6db20433c6bf458c2f2f.

use bun_jsc::array_buffer::MarkedArrayBuffer;
use bun_jsc::JSType;

t: [Unsoundness] `StdAllocator::free` accepts borrowed slices through a safe API
b:
What version of Bun is running?
Source verification against origin/main a9886150983872820ddf6db20433c6bf458c2f2f
What platform is your computer?
Linux 6.8.0-48-generic x86_64 x86_64
What steps can reproduce the bug?

use bun_alloc::StdAllocator;

let bytes = [1_u8, 2, 3, 4];

What is the expected behavior?
A safe deallocation API should require ownership/provenance of an allocation that came from the same allocator, or the raw deallocation entry point should be unsafe.

StdAllocator::free(&self, bytes: &[u8]) is safe and accepts any shared byte slice. It casts the slice to &mut [u8] and forwards it to the allocator vtable free callback, so safe Rust can ask the allocator to free stack, static, or otherwise non-owned memory.

t: TC39 decorators: superclass @addInitializer never fires; last decorator's cb fires twice on subclass
Piped stream errors are swallowed: body buffering resolves with truncated data instead of rejecting
b:
Found during review of #31963 (which fixes a GC rooting bug on this path but does not change error propagation).
When a piped ByteStream delivers StreamResult::Err (fetch body network failure, S3 download error), two pipe consumers drop the error value instead of propagating it:

ValueBufferer::on_stream_pipe (src/runtime/webcore/Body.rs): Err satisfies is_done(), so it calls (self.on_finished_buffering)(self.ctx, bytes, None, true) with None for the error. Buffering completes successfully with whatever bytes arrived before the failure instead of rejecting. The error channel exists (other paths pass Some(err), e.g. the abort path), the pipe path just never uses it.
RequestContext::on_pipe (src/runtime/server/RequestContext.rs): Err yields an empty slice(), the response is ended via end_stream, and the error value is discarded. The client sees a truncated but "complete" response.

Both match the Zig reference implementation (Body.zig onStreamPipe passes null; RequestContext.zig onPipe has no Err arm), so this is long-standing behavior, not a regression. Fixing it means deciding the user-visible semantics: buffered body promises (response.text() over a piped erroring stream) should presumably reject with the stream error, and a streamed HTTP response should terminate the connection abnormally rather than ending cleanly with truncated data.

t: Bun.build (bundler) cannot resolve a dependency imported from a symlinked file; no --preserve-symlinks equivalent
b:
What version of Bun
1.4.0-canary.1+a98861509 (macOS x64) — the Rust-rewrite canary.
Summary
Bun.build (and bun build) dereferences symlinks when resolving modules, then resolves a file's bare (npm) imports from the file's real path. When a file is consumed through a symlink — e.g. a shared-source folder symlinked into several projects — its node_modules live in the consuming project, not on the real path. So bundling fails with Could not resolve: "<pkg>" even though the dependency is installed in the consumer's node_modules.
The Bun runtime does NOT have this problem: it keeps the logical (symlink) path and resolves the dependency from the consumer's node_modules. The exact same import graph therefore runs fine under bun run but fails under Bun.build.
--preserve-symlinks (added in #18550, closing #4044) fixes only the runtime — it has no effect on Bun.build / bun build, and BuildConfig exposes no symlink/preserve option.
Reproduction
repo/
  shared/                      # shared source, NOT a package (no package.json, no node_modules)
    math.ts                    # imports a bare npm dep
  app/
    shared -> ../shared        # symlink
    node_modules/decimal.js    # dependency installed HERE
    package.json

shared/math.ts:
import { Decimal } from 'decimal.js';
export const x = new Decimal(1);
From app/:

bun -e "import('./shared/math.ts')" -> resolves (runtime keeps the symlink path -> app/node_modules)
bun build shared/math.ts --target=browser --outdir=out -> error: Could not resolve: "decimal.js", pointed at the REAL path repo/shared/math.ts
bun --preserve-symlinks build shared/math.ts ... -> same error (flag is runtime-only)

Expected
Bun.build should resolve a symlinked file's dependencies the way the runtime does (from the consumer that imported it), or expose a preserveSymlinks option on BuildConfig / a --preserve-symlinks the bundler honors.
Current workaround
A Bun.build plugin whose onResolve re-resolves bare imports originating inside the symlinked folder from the consumer root via Bun.resolveSync(spec, consumerRoot). Works, but every consumer must wire it; a first-class bundler option would remove the need.
Related

#4044 (runtime --preserve-symlinks request) — closed by #18550, runtime only
#22941 (Bun.build "Could not resolve", runtime works / bundler fails)

t: Adding middleware
bun install: UNKNOWN_CERTIFICATE_VERIFICATION_ERROR against a registry that bun's own fetch(), curl, and npm all verify
b:
What version of Bun is running?
1.3.8 — also reproduced on 1.3.14 (current latest).
What platform is your computer?
Linux x86_64 — GitHub-hosted self-hosted runner (Ubuntu-based hardened image).
What steps will reproduce the bug?
bun install against an internal JFrog Artifactory npm registry fails during manifest fetch:
error: UNKNOWN_CERTIFICATE_VERIFICATION_ERROR downloading package manifest vite

On the same machine, to the same host, every other client succeeds:

curl → HTTP 200; openssl s_client → Verify return code: 0 (ok). Full, valid chain: *.jfrog.io ← GeoTrust TLS RSA CA G1 ← DigiCert Global Root G2. The connection negotiates TLS 1.2 / RSASSA-PSS.
npm view vite → succeeds.
bun's own runtime fetch — bun -e 'fetch(url).then(r => console.log(r.status))' → 200 (TLS verifies fine).
bun install → fails with the certificate error above.

So bun's package-installer HTTP/TLS client rejects a chain that bun's runtime fetch, curl, and npm all accept on the same machine — which points at the installer's TLS path diverging from the runtime's.
What we ruled out

Not an invalid/incomplete chain — full 3-cert chain to a public DigiCert root; openssl verify code 0.
Not the system trust store — in a clean Ubuntu container, bun install succeeds against a registry whose CA is trusted only via update-ca-certificates.
--use-system-ca / NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 → no effect. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=<bundle.pem> → no effect.
Not version-specific — 1.3.8 and 1.3.14 both fail.
No proxy — direct connection, no HTTP(S)_PROXY set.

Hypothesis
The package installer's TLS/cert verification diverges from the runtime's fetch path — possibly around TLS 1.2 + RSASSA-PSS server certs, or it isn't consulting the same trust store the runtime uses.
Reproduction caveat
Reproduces reliably in our hardened CI against this registry, but we could not reproduce on a clean machine or against a generic public host — the installer-vs-runtime discrepancy on the same host is the strongest signal. Happy to run further diagnostics or test a patch.
Possibly related: #28804 (runtime fetch cert verification on macOS).

t: bun build --format=internal_bake_dev panics on JSON imports (Option::unwrap in print_dev_server_module)
b:
The standalone debug CLI path bun build --format=internal_bake_dev panics on any entry that imports a .json file:
echo '{"value":1}' > data.json
echo 'import data from "./data.json"; console.log(data.value)' > index.ts
bun build --format=internal_bake_dev index.ts
# => panic: called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value (print_dev_server_module)
Mechanism: for lazy-export (JSON) modules the linker's ESM lazy-export arm destroys the SLazyExport stmt, then print_dev_server_module's has_lazy_export special case unwraps it. The dev server itself is unaffected — Bun.serve dev bundles route JSON through the CJS lazy-export form (hmr.cjs.exports = ...) and print correctly; only the CLI-invoked internal format hits the destroyed-stmt path.
Found while verifying how JSON modules are wrapped in dev-server hot updates.

t: Dev server HMR: module flipping ESM->CJS gets require bound to undefined, dropping importer tracking
b:
In src/runtime/bake/hmr-module.ts, the ESM->CJS flip arms in loadModuleSync/loadModuleAsync build the replacement CJS module object with:
require: mod.require.bind(this),
At module scope this is undefined, so after a module flips from ESM to CJS across a hot update, its require calls loadModuleSync(id, true, undefined) — the importer parameter is lost and mod.importers.add(importer) never runs for that module's subsequent requires. Future edits to those dependencies won't propagate to the flipped module until a full reload.
The first-construction path correctly uses this.require.bind(this) inside the HMRModule constructor; only the flip arms are affected. Fix is mod.require.bind(mod) plus a test that flips a dep ESM->CJS and then edits one of its dependencies.
Noted while fixing stale CJS exports on hot reload; left unchanged there because it's a separate pre-existing defect.

t: PackageManager singleton is not thread-safe for concurrent auto-install from bundler and runtime
b:
Follow-up from #28531, which enabled auto-install for bun build / Bun.build().
The PackageManager process singleton is initialized once (initWithRuntimeOnce) and shared by every resolver. With #28531, both the bundler worker thread and the JS thread can reach it. Two consequences:


The PM's event_loop is bound at init time to the first caller's thread: either the VM's JS event loop or a MiniEventLoop wrapping the init thread's thread-local uws.Loop. A later auto-install from the other thread runs sleepUntil against a loop owned by a foreign thread. Sequentially this functions (epoll fds are process-wide), but a concurrent Bun.build() auto-install plus a runtime dynamic-import auto-install tick the same loop from two threads (uSockets loops are single-threaded; data race).


The event loop is not the only unsynchronized state: lockfile, task queues, the manifest cache, and pending counters are all accessed without locks, so concurrent auto-install from two threads races regardless of event-loop affinity.


In practice the two flows are almost always serialized (a build script rarely dynamic-imports an uninstalled package mid-build), but nothing enforces it.
Proper fix is architectural: per-thread PM instances, or serializing all auto-install through one owner thread. Raised in review of #28531 (see threads on PackageManager.zig event-loop init); out of scope for that PR.

t: Dev server: combined html+script rebuild stores the HTML module's import under an absolute path when the script specifier is bare
b:
What version of Bun is running? 1.4.0 (current main, also reproduces on the canary) What platform is your computer? Linux x64 What steps can reproduce the bug? Dev server with an HTML route whose script tag uses a bare relative specifier (

Hello

// script.ts console.log("v1"); // serve.ts import html from "./index.html"; export default { port: 0, static: { "/*": html }, fetch() { return new Response("nope", { status: 404 }); }, }; bun ./serve.ts, load / once. Write both index.html and script.ts in one watch batch (e.g. two writeFileSync calls back to back, or test/bake's dev.batchChanges()). Fetch / again and fetch the route's client bundle (/_bun/client/route-*.js). What is the expected behavior? The regenerated route bundle references script.ts by its incremental-graph key (script.ts), matching the module registry, and the page loads. What happens instead? The HTML module stored during the combined rebuild imports the script by absolute path, so the regenerated route bundle contains: "/tmp/dev/script.ts", 0, while the registry keys stay relative (script.ts). A browser that reloads the route after that rebuild fails to boot with: Error: Failed to load bundled module '/tmp/dev/script.ts'. This is not a dynamic import, and therefore is a bug in Bun's bundler. at throwNotFound (.../_bun/client/index-*.js) at loadModuleAsync at parseEsmDependencies and Available modules: [ 'index.html', 'script.ts', 'bun:wrap', 'bun:bake/client' ]. Notes from bisecting the conditions: Only happens when the script is an entry point of the same rebuild as the HTML file (combined watch batch). The initial bundle and html-only or script-only rebuilds produce relative keys. Only happens with a bare specifier (src="script.ts"). With src="./script.ts" the keys stay relative in all cases. Reachable by end users on current main: the combined rebuild's hot update is not accepted by the HMR client (HTML root module), so the client full-reloads into the broken bundle. Found while adding test coverage for #31908 in #31915; the regression test there uses ./script.ts to avoid this bug and links back to this issue.
